items.title: FIFA : Gianni Infantino renonce à son projet d'ouverture aux investisseurs privés
items.description: Face à une contestation grandissante, Gianni Infantino a finalement renoncé à son projet d'ouverture des activités commerciales de la FIFA à des investisseurs privés. Dans un communiqué publié samedi, le président de l'instance mondiale a annoncé l'abandon de FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), reconnaissant que cette initiative avait profondément divisé les fédérations. « Après avoir écouté attentivement tous les points de vue, il est devenu clair que le projet a créé des divisions qui ne sont plus dans l'intérêt de l'objectif initial. Notre but a toujours été, et sera toujours, d'unir et de progresser. La proposition ne sera donc pas retenue », a déclaré Gianni Infantino. Présenté cette semaine, le projet prévoyait la création d'une nouvelle société commerciale, FIFA Forward Enterprise, chargée de gérer une partie des activités commerciales et événementielles de la FIFA. L'objectif affiché était de porter à 10 milliards de dollars les investissements consacrés au développement du football au cours des quatre prochaines années. Pour financer cette ambition, la FIFA envisageait de céder jusqu'à 20 % de cette nouvelle structure à des investisseurs privés, avec l'espoir de lever environ 4,2 milliards de dollars. L'annonce avait toutefois provoqué une vive opposition. L'UEFA avait menacé de boycotter les compétitions organisées par la FIFA, y compris la Coupe du monde, si le projet était maintenu. La Concacaf avait également rejeté la proposition, tandis que la Confédération asiatique (AFC) avait regretté l'absence d'un consensus suffisant autour de cette réforme. Les confédérations africaine (CAF) et océanienne avaient, de leur côté, appelé leurs fédérations membres à examiner le projet avant de se prononcer, alors que la Conmebol réclamait davantage d'explications. Un projet au cœur de nombreuses critiques Au-delà des inquiétudes liées à une possible marchandisation du football, plusieurs responsables dénonçaient également la méthode employée par la FIFA. Le projet prévoyait notamment qu'en cas d'adoption, chacune des 211 fédérations membres puisse bénéficier d'un financement exceptionnel de 20 millions de dollars en 2027, tandis que les dotations du programme FIFA Forward auraient été relevées de 8 à 20 millions de dollars pour la période 2027-2030. Certains dirigeants, à l'image de la présidente de la Fédération norvégienne, Lise Klaveness, avaient dénoncé une forme de pression financière, estimant que la FIFA n'avait pas besoin de recourir à des investisseurs privés compte tenu de ses importantes réserves. Ce revirement intervient quelques heures seulement après la démission de Carlos Cordeiro, principal conseiller de Gianni Infantino, qui s'était publiquement opposé au projet, le qualifiant de « mauvaise affaire pour le football ». Fragilisé par cette fronde, le président de la FIFA choisit finalement de retirer une réforme qui aura suscité une opposition rare au sein du football mondial, à moins d'un an de l'élection présidentielle de mars 2027, pour laquelle il demeure, à ce stade, le seul candidat déclaré. The post FIFA : Gianni Infantino renonce à son projet d'ouverture aux investisseurs privés appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Alaafin demands apology from professor over ‘late arrival’ remark at event
items.description: By Adeola Badru Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Akeem Owoade, has demanded an apology and retraction from Professor Ademola Dasylva over comments alleging that the monarch arrived three hours late to the inauguration of the Alaafin’s Institute of Yoruba Studies at Emmanuel Alayande University of Education, Oyo. In a statement issued by his Director of Media and Publicity, Bode Durojaiye, the monarch described the remarks attributed to the professor as “reckless”, insisting that his arrival was in line with an adjusted schedule already communicated to the organisers. Durojaiye said it was inaccurate and unfair to portray the Alaafin, Oba Abimbola Akeem Owoade I, as arriving late, stressing that the Palace had informed the university in advance that the monarch would be travelling with other paramount traditional rulers from outside Oyo State. “For the records, the original schedule proposed by the university indicated 11:00 a.m. as the time for His Imperial Majesty’s arrival. “However, before the commencement of the event, the Director of Administration of the Alaafin’s Palace formally communicated that the Alaafin would be arriving with other paramount Obas travelling from outside Oyo State,” the statement read. It added that the Palace made it “unequivocally clear” that the monarch’s entourage could not arrive before noon or 1:00 p.m., noting that the information was conveyed in good faith to allow proper planning. “This communication was not an afterthought. It was made deliberately and in good faith to enable proper planning. To therefore feign surprise and launch into public castigation is either a wilful disregard of facts or a deliberate act of provocation,” Durojaiye stated. The Palace further argued that the movement of the Alaafin involves established royal protocols and coordination with other traditional rulers, saying it was inappropriate to expect an imperial procession to conform to arrangements made without full consultation. “The Palace does not move in isolation. When the Alaafin moves, he moves with the dignity of Oyo, with the council, and often in concert with other crowns. To expect an imperial procession to conform to a timetable designed without full consultation is to misunderstand both monarchy and courtesy,” the statement said. Durojaiye also questioned the basis of Dasylva’s comments, maintaining that the professor was neither the convener of the event nor a member of the protocol team and was not privy to communications between the Palace and the university. “The honourable and scholarly path would have been to inquire from the organisers before rushing to the marketplace of public opinion with insults. A professor of repute is expected to embody circumspection, research and restraint,” he said. While acknowledging Dasylva’s contributions to Yoruba scholarship, the Palace insisted that criticism must be based on verified facts, warning against what it described as attacks on Yoruba traditional institutions. “We therefore demand retraction and apology for remarks made without due consultation and in disregard of prior communication from the Palace,” Durojaiye said. The Palace maintained that the Alaafin attended the event according to the schedule communicated to organisers and described the monarch’s presence at the inauguration as a demonstration of his commitment to Yoruba education, culture and scholarship. “The Alaafin did not come late. He came according to schedule, as duly communicated. To say otherwise is to bear false witness,” the statement added. The post Alaafin demands apology from professor over ‘late arrival’ remark at event appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Portable apologises to fans after Charles Okocha boxing drama
items.description: By Enitan Abdultawab Street-pop singer Habeeb Okikiola, popularly known as Portable, has apologised to fans and organisers after walking out of his celebrity boxing rematch against Nollywood actor Charles Okocha, a decision that led to his disqualification on Friday night. In a statement released on Saturday through his management, Zeh Nation/Dr Zeh, the singer expressed regret over the abrupt end to the highly anticipated bout and apologised to everyone affected by the incident. “We sincerely apologise to the organisers, Balmoral Group, the entire event team, our fans, friends, family, and everyone who came out to support Portable at tonight’s celebrity boxing event,” the statement read. The management acknowledged the disappointment caused by Portable’s decision to quit after the opening round but appealed to Nigerians to respect his perspective. “We understand the disappointment caused by the outcome of the fight and by Portable’s decision to step away after the first round. While emotions can run high in moments like these, we respectfully ask everyone to respect his decision and perspective.” It also accepted responsibility for the controversy, adding that the team remained grateful for the support shown to the singer. “On behalf of Portable’s management, we take full responsibility for the disappointment this may have caused. We remain grateful for the unwavering love and support shown to him throughout this journey.” The management further thanked Balmoral Group for organising the event despite its dramatic conclusion. “We appreciate Balmoral Group and everyone involved for putting together a great event, and we sincerely apologise for any inconvenience caused.” Assuring fans that lessons had been learnt, the statement promised a better outing in future contests. “We have taken note of the feedback, and we are committed to learning from this experience. We promise to come back stronger and do better next time.” The rematch ended in controversy after Portable walked out before the end of the opening round. Although he later returned to the ring, officials disqualified him, handing victory to Okocha. Before explaining his actions earlier on Saturday, Portable had claimed he left the contest because Okocha bit and choked him during what he described as a wrestling-style altercation rather than a boxing match. The post Portable apologises to fans after Charles Okocha boxing drama appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Burkina : L’offensive agropastorale 2023-2025 propulse le PIB de 4,67 % et génère 91 000 emplois
items.description: Le Ministère de l'Agriculture, de l'Eau, des Ressources animales et halieutiques (MAERAH) a présenté, le 30 juillet 2026, le bilan complet de la mise en œuvre de l'Offensive agropastorale et halieutique (OAPH) 2023-2025. Fort de ces résultats probants, le Gouvernement a décidé de reconduire l'offensive pour une deuxième phase, prévue sur la période 2026-2028, avec un budget global dépassant les 840 milliards de F CFA, selon les données du ministère en charge de l'Agriculture. Lancée en 2023 pour atteindre la souveraineté alimentaire à l’horizon 2025, l’Offensive agropastorale et halieutique (OAPH) a mobilisé 273,99 milliards de FCFA sur les 592 milliards prévus. Avec des records de production sur le riz et le maïs, la création de plus de 91 000 emplois et une hausse de 4,67 % du PIB global, le bilan présenté par le Secrétaire technique Amos Kienou dessine les contours d’une transformation structurelle réussie, malgré des défis sécuritaires et un gap d’investissement privé. Selon Amos Kienou, globalement les objectifs de l'offensive ont été atteints Selon le Secrétaire technique Amos Kienou, l’objectif affiché dès le départ était d'assurer la souveraineté alimentaire du Burkina Faso en couvrant les besoins de consommation de la population tout en réduisant la dépendance aux importations. Pour ce faire, huit filières stratégiques ont été ciblées, parmi lesquelles le maïs, le riz, la pomme de terre, le poisson, la volaille et le bétail-viande, sur la base de critères précis comme l’importance dans la consommation nationale, le potentiel productif ou la capacité à générer des emplois décents pour les couches vulnérables. Des investissements massifs mais un appel manqué au privé Sur le plan financier, l’État a mobilisé 273,99 milliards de FCFA sur les 275 milliards attendus au titre du financement public, soit un taux de réalisation de 99,63 %. En revanche, la composante privée, estimée à 317 milliards de FCFA pour les périmètres irrigués, n’a enregistré aucun investissement, ce qui constitue le principal point d’ombre de cette phase. Quelques résultats projetés Le coût global prévisionnel de l’offensive était fixé à 592 milliards de FCFA, mais sans la contribution espérée du secteur privé, le dispositif a dû s’appuyer presque exclusivement sur les ressources publiques. Malgré un contexte sécuritaire toujours tendu dans certaines zones et une pression phytosanitaire modérée, les résultats physiques sont au rendez-vous. Selon les données du Ministère en charge de l'agriculture, les aménagements agricoles ont connu une progression significative avec 11 774 hectares de périmètres irrigués réhabilités ou nouvellement aménagés, et 41 275 hectares de bas-fonds, dont plus de 25 000 hectares réalisés par l’approche communautaire, jugée efficace et efficiente. Par ailleurs, 485 forages à gros débit ont été réalisés et des milliers d’équipements, tracteurs, motoculteurs, semoirs, motopompes, ont été mis à disposition des producteurs, tandis que 1 545 cages flottantes piscicoles ont été installées pour soutenir la filière poisson. Des records de production dans plusieurs filières À en croire Amos Kienou, les performances de production sont éloquentes. La filière riz a franchi le cap symbolique du million de tonnes de paddy, atteignant 1 013 000 tonnes, soit 101 % de l’objectif, avec une progression de 136,61 % par rapport à la moyenne 2020-2022. Le maïs affiche également un taux d’atteinte de 134 %, avec 2 680 000 tonnes produites. La pomme de terre, le poisson, la volaille et les petits ruminants enregistrent eux aussi des résultats notables, bien que certains objectifs comme celui du poisson (58,47 % atteint) ou du renouvellement des vergers de manguiers (63,4 %) restent partiellement à consolider. La relance du blé sur 2 526 hectares, pour une production de 9 806 tonnes en 2025, constitue une avancée majeure dans la diversification des cultures. Selon le responsable technique Amos Kienou, l’Offensive agropastorale et halieutique (OAPH) a également été marquée par des réformes institutionnelles profondes, avec la restructuration de la SONAGESS et la création de nouvelles entités comme la SOBIMAP, la CAMVET, l’ONBAH, le Conseil Burkinabè des Filières, Faso Kosam, Faso Guulgo, ainsi que les Brigades de mécanisation agricole. Sur le plan sanitaire, des campagnes de vaccination massive ont été menées contre les principales maladies animales et la pisciculture a bénéficié d’un traitement spécifique avec la gratuité de la vaccination contre la streptococcose. Des impacts significatifs sur l’économie et l’emploi Les impacts macroéconomiques et sociaux sont sensibles. « Le PIB agricole a progressé de 12,13 % et le PIB global de 4,67 %. Le taux de couverture des besoins céréaliers atteint désormais 124 %. En termes d’emploi, 91 027 postes ont été créés, dont 35,2 % occupés par des femmes, avec 26 202 emplois permanents. Les revenus des ménages ruraux ont augmenté de 7,5 % et ceux des ménages urbains de 2,5 %. L’offensive a aussi bénéficié à 4 724 personnes déplacées internes et à 289 Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, intégrés dans les différents dispositifs de production », a détaillé Monsieur Kienou. Un aperçu de la presse présenre à la conférence Au-delà des résultats, beaucoup de leçons ont été apprises, foi du Secrétaire technique. Il a révélé que l'expérience a montré que l’aménagement communautaire des bas-fonds est une approche pertinente, que le suivi rapproché des investissements améliore l’efficacité et que des cultures jusqu’alors marginales, le cacao, l'ananas, la vigne, la banane plantain, le tournesol, sont viables au Burkina Faso. Enfin, le représentant du Ministère en charge de l'agriculture a rassuré que la consolidation des acquis et la prise en compte des nouveaux défis, notamment l’attraction des investissements privés et la sécurisation durable des zones productives, seront au cœur de la prochaine étape de cette offensive pour une souveraineté alimentaire désormais à portée de main. Lire aussi : Offensive agropastorale : Le Burkina injecte près de 840 milliards de F CFA pour la période 2026-2028 Mathias KAM Minute.bf

items.title: Quetta coal mine explosion: Search and rescue operation concludes as last two bodies recovered
items.description: QUETTA: The bodies of the remaining two miners trapped following a methane gas explosion in a mine near Quetta were found on Saturday. The explosion occurred on Thursday at a private coal mine in the Sorange coalfield, about 30 kilometres northeast of Quetta. The methane gas explosion triggered a fire, caused the mine to collapse, and affected another nearby mine. Balochistan Chief Inspector of Mines Muhammad Atif confirmed to Dawn that “all 34 bodies of coal miners trapped” in the mines have been recovered. He added that the last two bodies were recovered after hectic search efforts. The bodies of 32 miners were recovered on Friday. Atif said both mines were sealed after the rescue operation was completed and a probe into the tragic incident has been ordered. “A team of mining experts has been formed, which has initiated a probe into the incident,” the official said. All of the miners hailed from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Shangla district, Atif said, adding that their bodies have been dispatched to their native villages. “Twenty-three miners who lost their lives belonged to Pirabad alone,” he added. Abid Yaar, president of the Shangla Coal Mine Workers Association, said on Friday that Mian Kalay in Pir Abad — from where at least 23 of the miners hailed — had become an epicentre of repeated coal mine tragedies. He added that the victims, aged between 17 and 25, belonged to the same families and were cousins or close relatives. According to Yaar, several of the deceased were orphans whose fathers had also lost their lives in previous coal mine accidents. Out of the 34 miners, 24 were working about 4,000 feet underground in the first mine where the methane gas explosion occurred, while the rest were working in another nearby mine. Deadly mine explosions are common in Balochistan, with stakeholders often pointing out the absence of essential safety protocols. Coal mining has historically been fraught with hazards, which are similar to those associated with the aftermath of natural disasters: suffocation, gas poisoning, roof collapse, rock burst, gas explosions and a plethora of lung diseases, including incurable diseases like coalworker’s pneumoconiosis, also known as black lung disease.

items.title: PML-N MNA Malik Iqbal Channar passes away at 76
items.description: LAHORE: MNA Malik Muhammad Iqbal Channar, who had been unwell for several weeks, passed away in Bahawalpur on Saturday. He was 76. According to the family, his funeral prayers will be offered at 6pm on Saturday at Bahawalpur Stadium. He was father of Punjab Assembly Deputy Speaker Malik Zaheer Iqbal Channar. Channar, who had served as a provincial minister and remained an influential PML-N leader in south Punjab for decades, was elected to the National Assembly from NA-168 Bahawalpur. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed profound grief over Channar’s demise and paid tribute to his political, social and public services. The prime minister described him as a sincere public representative, a committed and ideological PML-N worker, and a loyal companion of former premier Nawaz Sharif. “I had the privilege of knowing him personally and had the opportunity to work with him on several occasions when he served in my Punjab cabinet,” PM Shehbaz said, adding that Iqbal’s loyalty, dedication, public service and commitment would always be remembered. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also expressed deep sorrow over the lawmaker’s death and extended her heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family. She said Channar’s political and public services would be remembered for a long time. NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq expressed profound grief and sorrow over Channar’s demise, saying his death “deprived parliament of a sincere, dignified and people-oriented member”. Sadiq said Channar’s parliamentary, political and public service would always be remembered. He added that the deceased’s “contributions to national politics and the promotion of democratic traditions were invaluable”. The NA speaker also extended his heartfelt condolences and sympathies to the deceased’s son. “In this hour of grief, I stand in solidarity with the bereaved family,” he added. PML-N leader Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said that he was saddened to learn about Channar’s demise, terming it a great loss for the party and national politics.

items.title: Daddy Showkey: From ghetto to grace, celebrates 50 years on stage
items.description: …How Ajegunle, ‘Dyna’ miracle, Vanguard, Eko hotels shaped my journey …To honour on August 9 concert …’I once scavenged for aluminium to survive’ …Reveals how he created Galala sound, got the name ‘Showkey’ For Daddy Showkey, the journey has been one of survival, music, and miracles. On August 9, 2026, the pioneer of Galala music will mark 50 years on stage with a golden jubilee concert at Eko Hotel and Suites, Lagos, the same venue where it all started for him nearly five decades ago with an acrobatic performance at the hotel’s opening . “Eko Hotel opened in 1977, and I performed an acrobatic display during the opening ceremony,” he recalls. Ahead of the milestone event, the 56-year-old entertainer walked into the Vanguard headquarters in Apapa, Lagos, on Thursday evening with gaiety. The visit was more than courtesy. It was a homecoming of sorts: nostalgia and gratitude wrapped in one. The “ghetto soldier” with the signature dreadlocks used the moment to revisit memories that shaped his career and to thank Vanguard for its role in his rise. From picking aluminium in Ajegunle dustbins, to birthing Galala music, to making a promise to God about his community, Showkey said the journey has been nothing short of grace. Read on… By Onochie Anibeze, Ayo Onikoyi & Benjamin Njoku We heard you’re celebrating 50 years on stage, and we decided to bring you to Vanguard because we also want to celebrate you. Tell us about the milestone concert? I will be celebrating 50 years on stage on August 9 at Eko Hotel and Suites, Lagos. I chose Eko Hotel because it is part of my journey and my story. Eko Hotel opened in 1977, and I performed an acrobatic display during the opening ceremony. By the grace of God, there was a Banquet Manager there, Mr. Ben, who always gave me a chance to perform whenever they had events. So, Eko Hotel has always been part of my story. My journey actually started in 1976, at Gondola, Bar Beach, and Panorama. I was just six years old then. Sometimes, people would ask me, “How old are you?” I will be 56 on August 4. People think it is impossible to discover a child’s talent at a young age, but I am living proof that it is possible. That is why I always tell parents that documenting their children’s talents and growth is very important. Back then, we only had photographs to capture memories. Today, when I look back, I always tell people to go through my old newspaper interviews. I have consistently said I started entertainment in 1976, because that was when I began appearing on television. But if I wanted to count from when I first started entertaining people on the streets of Ajegunle, it would have been even earlier. My journey has simply been from ghetto to grace. Would you like to recall some of those early days in Ajegunle? Entertainment-wise, I can remember that around the 80s, I formed a group called Barrel Paragon Dancers. Before I turned 10, I was already an established entertainer. People paid me to perform at events. We performed together until about 1983. At the same time, I was also acting part-time. I appeared in “The Village Headmaster” as an acrobat. The person who introduced me to the production was Dejumo Lewis. I was also part of the later production of “The Village Headmaster”. My first manager, Mr. Bod Alaba, who acted the part of journalist Emeka in “The Village Headmaster” helped secure performance opportunities for me. Mr John Chukwu (J.C.) and Mr. Jimmy Johnson, popularly known as Okoro, also booked shows for me. When Jimmy Johnson launched his album in 1983, I performed acrobatics at the event. So, even if I decide to count only from when I became active professionally, it is still more than 40 years as a musician. But I don’t just see myself as a musician. I see myself as an entertainer. Acrobatics is entertainment too. Many of the veteran musicians who knew me as a child performer are still surprised whenever they see me today. Someone like veteran actor Jide Kosoko played an important role in my journey. At the time, he worked at Eldatech, a candle manufacturing company near my school. I attended Dr. Lucas School in Kirikiri. One day, he saw me performing acrobatics during our inter-house sports competition. By then, I had stopped appearing on television because I had lost contact with my managers. Uncle Jide invited me to the National Theatre, where they were reorganizing the Ojo Ladipo Theatre after the death of Baba Mero. Through him, I met several theatre veterans, including Mama Bibi Alice Ambebo. He introduced me as his boy, and they began taking me to different performances and events. From there, I continued performing and working with several theatre practitioners. Honestly, I don’t even know where to begin counting the journey. All I know is that I started entertainment in 1976, and if you count from then until now, it is 50 years. It is my Golden Jubilee, and I believe it is worth celebrating. What should we expect on that day? First of all, the Special Guest of Honour will be my mother. My mum was a teacher, and she supported me despite what people were saying. Many people would ask her, “How can the son of a teacher not be in school?” I also have to appreciate some of my teachers, especially Mrs. Moneke, who went to meet my mother and told her, “Don’t force him. If this is what he wants to do, let him pursue it.” Looking back today, I went through a lot. But I believe God used my mother to shape my journey. I lost my father in 1978, when I was just eight years old. So, my mum had to carry the burden of raising us alone. She went through a lot of hardship. I am the last child of my mother. People constantly questioned her because I wasn’t following the conventional path of staying in school. But she always defended me. She would simply say, “He’s a special child.” Today, many of those same people now tell my mother, “You were right. He truly is a special child.” That is one of the reasons she is the Special Guest of Honour. It will also be the first time in her life that she will sit in the audience and watch me perform live on stage. It will be her first time ever? Yes. That is why she is my Special Guest of Honour. What is the story behind your song ‘Dyna (If You See My Mama)’? The song “Dyna” is based on a true-life story. Back in 1996, before I travelled to Germany, a woman named Dyna came to meet me. She had been married for nine years without having a child, and there was a lot of pressure from her husband’s family. Some people even believed all kinds of superstitions about why she couldn’t conceive. She came to me crying and asked me to speak to her husband. She told me she wasn’t against him marrying another wife if that would make him happy. Her only request was that he shouldn’t send her away because she had nowhere else to go. At first, I wondered why she came to me because I wasn’t a pastor. But I promised to visit their home and speak with her husband. When I got to their house, I knocked on the door and it was her husband who opened it. The moment he saw me, he shouted, “Showkey Baba!” He welcomed me warmly and invited me inside. As soon as I entered their living room, I saw a large portrait of myself hanging on the wall. Dyna had already told me that her husband was one of my biggest fans, so she believed he would listen to me. I explained why I had come. I told him his wife had shared with me that they had been married for nine years without a child and that there was pressure from members of the family. The husband simply said, “Don’t mind my mother and my sisters. They are only saying those things because they want children.” I told them to buy ‘pelebe (a local drink)’. When they brought it, I poured a little on the ground and prayed. I declared that before another three months passed, Dyna would become pregnant. After praying, I left. Not long after that, I travelled to Germany. Exactly three months later, while I was at a train station in Germany, I received a phone call informing me that Dyna was pregnant. I was overjoyed. I bought drinks right there and celebrated because God had answered their prayers. When I returned to Nigeria, I went back to meet the couple and asked for their permission to turn their story into a song. Her husband gladly agreed. One of the happiest days of my life was when Dyna gave birth to a baby boy. They named him John, after me. That day remains one of the greatest honours I have ever received. I was the chairman of the naming ceremony. The husband and wife even made an outfit for me from the same fabric they wore. He also gave me money to spray during the celebration. As the celebration continued, people started spraying money on me because they believed God had used me in their testimony. Women who had not yet conceived came to me asking me to pray for them as well. I also have to appreciate the late Chief Raymond Dokpesi. He believed strongly in that song and insisted it would change lives. He said it would give hope to many women and help people understand that only God gives children. Many people get married expecting to have children immediately, but they don’t always know what challenges a couple may be facing. That song became a message of hope and also a way of standing up for women who were unfairly blamed for infertility. The song changed my life too. Everywhere I go in the world, people still talk about it. Dyna and her husband now live in the United States, and after that first child, God blessed them with four more children. Apart from Dyna’s testimony, many other women have come to me asking me to pray for them just as I prayed for her. I thank God for everything He has done. So they are in the United States now and doing well? Yes, they have been there for a long time. Their first son is almost 30 years old now. My own son is 29, while Dyna’s son is about 30. It has truly been a long journey. What a remarkable story. Back to the present day, Vanguard is happy to celebrate your achievements. Many of today’s biggest stars; Burna Boy, Davido and Wizkid show you a great deal of respect whenever they run into you. Perhaps it’s because you started the revolution? I wouldn’t say it’s because I started the revolution. I believe that if you respect yourself, people will respect you. I grew up among Yoruba people, and there’s a saying that teaches you to respect others so they will respect you too. I’ve always lived by that principle. I don’t see myself as being above anyone. Some people mistake humility for weakness, but I don’t. To me, humility is strength. If you can relate with people genuinely, they’ll appreciate you for who you are. The people who think humility is weakness are the ones who don’t really understand it. Sometimes, when you think you’re too important, that’s when you become nothing. But do they really respect you? Why wouldn’t they? If I respect myself and respect others, they’ll respect me too. What would you say about the Nigerian music industry today? First of all, I thank God for this new generation of artists. They’ve taken Nigerian music to the level we dreamed about during our own time. They’ve done incredibly well. If you travel outside Nigeria and see how our music is celebrated around the world, you’ll thank God. Nigerian music has become a global force, and I’m proud of what they’ve achieved. Everything about you reflects Ajegunle. You were never ashamed to identify with the community. It shaped your music, your character and your career. Does it worry you that some people say Ajegunle music has disappeared? No. I think that’s a wrong impression. Ajegunle music hasn’t disappeared. Look at Don Jazzy. He’s from Ajegunle. Wizkid that you’re talking about, also has roots in Ajegunle. People say different things, but what I always tell people is this: music doesn’t belong to any particular place or tribe. Music has no language. Someone can be Igbo and perform Yoruba music. What matters is the rhythm and the message. Every day, a child is born with talent. Every single day, new talents emerge, regardless of where they come from. Talent isn’t limited by geography. What matters is recognizing it, developing it and giving it the opportunity to grow. That’s what I believe, and that’s the story of my own journey. You also survived serial attacks on you! That happened around 2014 or 2015. People said it was a robbery, but it wasn’t. They came to my house to assassinate me. By the grace of God, they didn’t find me. As we say, they only touched the back of my leg (laughs). About three months later, they traced me again. We got to a filling station in Agidingbi, and that was where they shot at my car. By the grace of God, we’re still alive. They destroyed the car, but life is what matters, not the car. Who sent those assassins? It’s a long story. I can’t explain it because you don’t always know who your enemies are. You may be going about your life without knowing who is jealous of you or who has something against you. I can’t point to anyone and say, this person did it. But if people come to your house, kill someone there, and then six months later they trace you again and shoot at you at a filling station, that’s not robbery. It means they were following you. I thank God that we’re alive. As for me, I don’t have enemies. I don’t fight anybody. They’re the ones fighting themselves. As you celebrate 50 years on stage at Eko Hotel, will this mark the beginning of a new chapter for you? And looking at the lineup, many of the performers are artists from your generation. What’s the idea behind that? I wouldn’t say they’re all from my generation. They’re great entertainers, and some of them came after me. If you’re talking strictly about my generation, you won’t even find many of them on the lineup. Let’s take 2Baba, for example. He came after me, but he’s someone who has always appreciated the little role I played in his career. Whenever he sees me, he reminds me of the things I did for him. Sometimes, I don’t even remember them myself, but he does. African China will be there. 9ice will also perform. Oritse Femi, King Saheed Osupa, Flectaman, Danfo Drivers, Marvelous Benjy, Tony Tetuila, Korede Bello, Iyanya, and Pasuma, among others, will join me on stage. A lot of great entertainers will be there. Earlier, you spoke about changing people’s perception of Ajegunle. Can you tell us more about that? The reason I decided to fight for the children of my neighbourhood was because of the impression people had about Ajegunle. It wasn’t because Ajegunle was better than other places or because other communities didn’t have talented people. Back then, if you told people you were from Ajegunle, they immediately labelled you an armed robber or a criminal. Before me, many talented people had already come out of Ajegunle, but they were afraid to identify themselves with the community. There were great footballers and other successful people who would rather say they were from Apapa than admit they came from Ajegunle. I wasn’t just born in Ajegunle, I grew up with the good, the bad and the ugly. I experienced everything that came with living there. I also experienced the stigma firsthand. After I finished secondary school in 1989, I applied for a job. The moment they saw my home address, they accused me of stealing a German Shepherd dog. At that time, I didn’t even know there were different breeds of dogs. We simply called every foreign dog a “police dog.” They arrested me, beat me and took me to Apapa Police Station simply because they saw “Ajegunle” on my application. There was a police woman who recognised me. She knew me as the young boy who performed acrobatics in the market and entertained people for money. She told the others, “This boy isn’t a thief.” She admitted that pickpockets sometimes operated around places where I performed, but she insisted I wasn’t one of them. While I was still at the station, someone arrived with the dog they claimed I had stolen. By then, the dog had already bitten me. That experience changed my life. I made a promise to God that if I ever became successful, I would change the way people viewed Ajegunle. Today, many people proudly identify with their neighbourhoods. People now openly say they’re from Mushin, Surulere or wherever they come from. Before then, many people were ashamed to do that because communities like Ajegunle and Mushin were stereotyped. One of my greatest achievements is helping people become proud of where they come from. Be proud of your family. Be proud of your roots, even if your parents didn’t have money. I grew up around refuse dumps. I scavenged for aluminium in dustbins just to survive. I remember reading one of your interviews where you told the late Ogbonna Amadi that you knew you would become a star the day Vanguard published your story? Vanguard played a major role in my life. The first time my elder brother and I came to Vanguard, we didn’t know anyone except Sunday Areh because we were from the same area. He introduced us to people in the newsroom. One of the photographers saw me and jokingly asked how I could be Sunday Areh’s younger brother when I spoke Yoruba so fluently. He took my photograph, and that moment changed my life. People like Ogbonna Amadi, Sunday Areh, Blessyn Okpowo, the late Victor Omoregie and many others at Vanguard supported me. Vanguard wasn’t just reporting my story, it was also helping me survive. The late Ogbonna Amadi mentored me. He shaped me into the person people know today. Whenever I tried to force myself to speak English, he would stop me and say, “No. Express yourself naturally. Speak Pidgin.” I remember when I won my first award in 1994. I was invited to a dinner at the Sheraton Hotel. They served a buffet and placed a fork and knife in front of me. I called Ogbonna and told him I didn’t know how to use cutlery. He tried explaining it over the phone, but I still couldn’t figure it out. Eventually, I quietly asked one of the waiters for help. Those are memories I can never forget. Another journalist who made a major impact on me was Yinka Bola of FAME magazine. He wrote a headline that has stayed with me ever since: “From Ghetto to Grace.” I still have that magazine in my house today. That’s why I always tell people my story isn’t just about Ajegunle. It’s about giving hope to children who think where they come from determines where they’ll end up. You can become somebody regardless of your background. That’s why, even today, I still go back to Ajegunle. Fifty years on stage is a major milestone. Looking back at your very first performance, what would you say is the biggest difference between the Showkey of that time and the Showkey of today? Back then, there was no Daddy Showkey. I was known as John Odafe, also called Professor Boy. The name “Showkey” actually came from my grandmother and my uncle. They used to call me “Showkid” because I was a little boy who was always entertaining people. Overtime, “Showkid” evolved into “Showkey.” The biggest difference between then and now is the responsibility that came with fame. Music opened many doors for me and made me popular. The late Ras Kimono was the first person who paid me as a musician. He invited me to perform at a show, and afterwards, they handed me an envelope containing ₦15,000. At that time, it was a huge amount of money. I had never received that kind of money before from performing. I was so excited that when I got back to Ajegunle, I told everyone at the drinking spot to keep drinking because I had money. As Daddy Showkey, fame came with a lot of responsibilities. When I was younger, I didn’t have those responsibilities. Some people exploited me along the way, but looking back now, I believe they were also part of my growth. If they hadn’t given me those opportunities, even under those circumstances, I might not be where I am today. So, I thank God for the journey. You are credited with birthing ‘Galala’. How did you create the movement? ‘Galala’ simply means growth and expansion. ‘Galala’ is the music, while ‘Konto’ is the dance. I wanted something that would distinguish my music from traditional reggae, even though reggae was the foundation of my sound. I blended reggae with highlife and other traditional Nigerian musical influences to create something unique. My first album was an experiment. I tried a bit of Fuji, rap and several other styles just to discover what connected most with people. That’s how ‘Galala’ was born. The dance itself came from boxing because I used to be a boxer. Some of the movements we used in the ring eventually became dance steps. We also decided to sing reggae in Nigerian Pidgin English rather than copying the Jamaican style. That became our identity, and that’s why we called it ‘Galala’. If you had to choose five songs that best define Daddy Showkey’s career, which ones would they be? I don’t like choosing favourites because every song is part of my creativity. Each song carries its own message, and different listeners connect with different songs in different ways. Sometimes, people focus on the melody, while others pay attention to the lyrics. For example, when people hear “Shine Your Eyes,” some misunderstand the message. I’m not encouraging people to do wrong things. I’m simply telling them to be alert and aware of what’s happening around them. Everyone interprets music differently, but as the songwriter, I know the message behind every lyric. Today, some people may not even pay attention to lyrics. They simply enjoy the beat. That’s the trend with many younger listeners. What’s your opinion of today’s music, especially Afrobeats? How different is it from your own style? Every generation listens to the kind of music it enjoys. Today’s audience is different. Many people are looking for songs that make them feel good or get them excited, so musicians create music that reflects what the audience wants. If you’re talking strictly about lyrical content, I don’t believe today’s music is necessarily stronger than the music of earlier generations. The post Daddy Showkey: From ghetto to grace, celebrates 50 years on stage appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tinubu rejected bishops’ assessment of economy, insecurity – Onaiyekan
items.description: Archbishop Emeritus of the Catholic Archdiocese of Abuja, John Onaiyekan, says President Bola Tinubu disagreed with the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria over its assessment of the country’s economy, insecurity and political climate during their recent meeting at the Presidential Villa. Tinubu hosted the bishops on July 28, 2026, after they expressed concerns about worsening economic conditions, insecurity and the state of Nigeria’s democracy. Speaking on Prime Time on Arise News on Friday, Onaiyekan said the President rejected the bishops’ position and insisted that his administration was performing well. “When the nation is bleeding, you cannot expect a polite meeting with the Head of State. We told him the economy is not helping our poor people; he told us the economy is doing fine. Frankly speaking, he told us quite clearly that he did not agree with us,” Onaiyekan said. He added, “We didn’t expect him to agree with us. We have done our duty, we have delivered our message, and we have a feeling that somehow, along the line, somebody will show him a few of the things we said.” The cleric said the memorandum presented to the President reflected the collective position of the Catholic Bishops’ Conference after wide consultations across the country. “We are not politicians running for office. We are religious leaders who feel we have a duty not just to preach our doctrines but also to address the lives of our people,” he said. Onaiyekan noted that the bishops intentionally presented the harsh realities facing Nigerians rather than offering a favourable picture of the country. He said they were satisfied that Tinubu listened because he responded directly to the issues raised. The former Abuja archbishop, however, expressed concern that many people within government were unwilling to speak frankly to the President, describing the lack of honest feedback as a major national problem. On the political situation, Onaiyekan defended the bishops’ warning against what they called the creeping danger of a one-party dominant state, arguing that democracy depends on credible elections and a level playing field for all political actors. Responding to Tinubu’s defence of the Independent National Electoral Commission, he maintained that public doubts about the commission’s neutrality would persist as long as its leadership continued to be appointed by the President. He called for reforms to strengthen confidence in the electoral process and urged Tinubu to protect democratic institutions, saying Nigerians deserved better governance and that government should focus more on solving the country’s problems than celebrating its achievements. items.title: Xavier Moreau : «Emmanuel Macron a un problème personnel avec RT»
items.description: « RT a ete la chaîne des Gilets jaunes ». Ce 31 juillet sur notre antenne, Xavier Moreau, directeur de Strapol, est revenu sur « l'un des episodes » ayant pu alimenter l'animosite que le locataire de l'elysee voue a l'encontre de la chaîne au logo vert, torpillee au printemps 2023 , precipitant au chomage une centaine de salaries, dont une cinquantaine de journalistes. « J'etais dans la rue avec les Gilets jaunes sur les Champs-elysees, toutes les grandes chaînes de television francaises se cachaient en haut des bâtiments, parce que la foule voulait les lyncher parce qu'ils etaient les medias du regime alors que RT France etait applaudi, cheri, par les manifestants », s'est rappele ce saint-cyrien. « Donc, je pense qu'Emmanuel Macron a un probleme personnel avec RT. Je pense que, de toute maniere, le regime actuel a un probleme personnel avec toute forme de liberte d'expression », a rencheri Xavier Moreau, confiant etre « globalement assez pessimiste » quant a une possibilite d'amelioration de la situation apres un depart de l'actuel president de l'elysee en 2027. « Vis-a-vis de la Russie, c'est le meme discours partout » « Cette censure, ce matraquage, cette repression ca fonctionne… », a-t-il par ailleurs estime avant de poursuivre : « les partis qui sont encore sur la liste de ceux qui peuvent l'emporter en 2027 sont des partis du systeme – du RN a la LFI en passant par les multiples candidats qui veulent recuperer l'heritage […] d'Emmanuel Macron – en gros, vis-a-vis de la Russie, c'est le meme discours partout ». evoquant un « regime aux abois », il a par ailleurs depeint les individus actuellement au pouvoir comme ne voulant « pas lâcher le morceau », notamment via cette « chape de plomb » que represente a ses yeux l'interdiction des reseaux sociaux visant les mineurs de moins de 15 ans. « Il n'y a pas de quoi etre fiere », a estime celui qui est lui-meme sous le coup de sanctions de Bruxelles, depuis fin 2025, pour ses opinions, renvoyant notamment a Loi des suspects. Vote en pleine Terreur, ce texte ordonnait l'arrestation des « Gens suspects » dans une periode marquee par la paranoïa revolutionnaire, notamment a l'encontre de complots, tant reels qu'imaginaires. « Les gens qui nous sanctionnent, sans proces, sans avocat – qui contredisent toutes nos institutions – considerent qu'ils sont vertueux et que leur vertu doit nous etre appliquee par la terreur », a fustige Xavier Moreau, apres avoir regrette une « tradition politique » francaise et rappele ces mots de Robespierre lorsqu'il invoquait « la terreur, sans laquelle la vertu est impuissante ». « La terreur ca consiste a vous faire sortir de la citoyennete, a vous faire sortir de vos droits les plus fondamentaux : liberte d'expression – article 19 de la Declaration des droit de l'homme – inalienabilite de la propriete, article 17, la liberte de circulation… », a-t-il finalement egrene.

items.title: Search operation to locate 7 climbers missing after Broad Peak avalanche resumes
items.description: GILGIT: A search and rescue operation to locate seven climbers part of a 10-member team that went missing after an avalanche at Broad Peak earlier this week resumed on Saturday morning. The operation was suspended late Friday due to adverse weather conditions in the region. The bodies of three climbers — Oman’s Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy, Nepal’s Pur Bahadur Gurung and American Mallory Geis — were found on Friday and airlifted to Skardu. The missing climbers include five from Nepal, including renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja, Kili Pemba Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Gyalu Sherpa. Pakistan’s climber Sohail Sakhi and China’s Wang Zhong are also among those missing. According to the local administration, a three-member civil rescue team, led by renowned mountaineer Sarbaz Khan, was taking part in the search and rescue operation. The team started their ground mission again on Saturday morning to locate the seven missing climbers. Additionally, Nepali climbers present at the basecamp with other expedition teams were also taking part in the operation. Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) President Major General Irfan Arshad told Dawn that the search operation was underway at Broad Peak. He said Pakistan Army helicopters were also heading towards the area where the climbers went missing. The club’s general secretary, Ayaz Shigri, also told Dawn that the rescue operation was being carried out with support of army helicopters. He said that during the operation the rescue teams had identified the presence of more climbers at an altitude of 6,000m through drone footage. “Mountain terrain, adverse weather, snow avalanche risks and snowfall create difficulties for rescue team members,” he said. According to Nepali media , renowned Nepali mountaineer Mingma David Sherpa arrived in Pakistan to assist the search and rescue operation. David travelled from Nepal to join the ongoing efforts to locate Purja and the other missing climbers. The avalanche struck while the mountaineers were on a mission to summit Broad Peak (8,047 metres, 26,400 feet) on Thursday while the team was ascending at an altitude of around 6,600 metres, according to regional authorities. The team was last in contact on Thursday morning, an official statement said, with reports emerging that evening of the powerful avalanche. “Data from their tracking devices indicates that they were thrown hundreds of metres down the mountainside,” Naila Kiani, from Pakistan’s Alpine Club, told Le Monde newspaper. Additional input from AFP

items.title: Livestream: Newsfile discusses Supreme Court rulings, Sedinam Tamakloe’s legal twist, and OSP powers
items.description: This Saturday, JoyNews’ flagship current affairs programme, Newsfile , discusses another compelling edition as a distinguished panel dissects some of the most consequential legal, constitutional, and governance developments shaping Ghana’s national discourse. Hosted by Samson Lardy Anyenini, the four-hour live broadcast—from 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM—will examine landmark Supreme Court decisions, the dramatic legal developments surrounding former MASLOC CEO Sedinam Tamakloe Attionu, and the constitutional implications of recent judicial pronouncements. 78 Charges Fall: Extradited fugitive Sedinam Tamakloe freed from 10-year jail sentence The panel will analyse the Court of Appeal’s decision that overturned the conviction of former MASLOC Chief Executive Sedinam Tamakloe Attionu, resulting in the collapse of 78 charges and the setting aside of her 10-year prison sentence after her extradition to Ghana. The discussion will explore the legal reasoning behind the judgment, its implications for the justice system, and what it means for future high-profile corruption prosecutions. Supreme Court on CRC: Delegate system declared unconstitutional; Constitutional Review Commission report under scrutiny Attention will turn to the Supreme Court’s ruling declaring aspects of the Constitutional Review Commission’s delegate system unconstitutional, alongside concerns that recommendations from the Commission’s report were selectively adopted. The conversation will assess the constitutional significance of the judgment and its implications for future governance reforms and constitutional amendments. OSP Powers Intact: Supreme Court unanimously dismisses controversial suit The programme will also examine the Supreme Court’s unanimous dismissal of a suit challenging the powers of the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP). The panel will discuss the implications of the ruling for Ghana’s anti-corruption architecture, prosecutorial independence, and the OSP’s ongoing investigations. The panel features Gary Nimako Marfo – Director, Legal Affairs, New Patriotic Party (NPP) Inusah Fuseini – Former Member of Parliament for Tamale Central and Former Minister for Lands and Natural Resources Mary Awelana Addah – Executive Director, Transparency International Ghana Manasseh Azure Awuni – Investigative Journalist Oliver Barker-Vormawor – Constitutional Rights and Policy Strategy Advisor, Democracy Hub With legal accountability, constitutional governance, and anti-corruption efforts taking centre stage, this edition promises robust analysis and spirited debate from some of the country’s leading legal minds, governance experts, and public policy advocates. Listeners and viewers can follow the discussion live on Joy 99.7 FM , Luv 99.5 FM , and the JoyNews television channel on DStv Channel 421 and GOtv Channel 125 . The programme will also be available across major podcast platforms for on-demand listening.

items.title: Activists held in Lahore for holding pro-Kashmir demonstration
items.description: LAHORE: Activists of the Haqooq-i-Khalq Party were arrested on Friday while holding a peaceful demonstration outside the press club to show solidarity with the Joint Action Committee of AJK. However, a party spokesperson says that all the detainees have been released on the condition that there will be no demonstration on Saturday (today). Activist Farooq Tariq was also among those arrested during the peaceful solidarity protest with the people of Kashmir. He was dragged, harassed and forcibly taken away in a police van. Along with him, Punjab Police arrested dozens of other protesters, including Muzammil Kakar and Hussain Jameel Faridi. The HKP expressed its deep concerns on the arrests as there was no information about the whereabouts of Farooq Tariq or other detainees. The party demanded their immediate release and called on the authorities to disclose their whereabouts without delay. The Pakistan Kissan Rabita Committee (PKRC) also strongly condemned the arbitrary arrest of its Federal Committee member, Farooq Tariq. Police dispersed the peaceful gathering, dragging and harassing protesters before forcing them into police vans. Among those arrested are members of Haqooq-e-Khalq Party, Khalq Youth Front and Progressive Students Collective, including Haris Azad, Zahid Ali, Ali Raza, Ali Abdullah, Rai Ali Aftab, Sher Ali, and others. The PKRC said, “The incommunicado detention is unacceptable and it violates the constitutional rights to peaceful assembly, freedom of expression, and political dissent”. Later, Farooq Tariq shared a status on his social media accounts, saying, “We are rescheduling today’s protest. We will organise it again. Please do not go to Shimla Hill (press club) now. Next time we will come with permission”. The protest was organised in solidarity with the Azad Jammu & Kashmir’s Joint Awami Action Committee demanding “democratic rights, economic justice, and accountable governance”. The committee in Kashmir has been protesting in Rawalakot and other cities of Azad Kashmir since early June. It claims that 30 protesters had been killed by the crackdown by armed forces since the polling day on July 27. The committee’s main demand includes abolition of 12 assembly seats for Kashmiris living in various cities of Pakistan. The PKRC has also demanded an end to the criminalisation of peaceful political activity and solidarity protests, respect for the constitutional rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly. Published in Dawn, August 1st, 2026

items.title: Tyla removes Lagos from world tour after backlash
items.description: South African singer Tyla has removed Lagos from the schedule of her upcoming A Pop world tour following online backlash from some Nigerians over renewed reports of xenophobic attacks against Nigerians in South Africa. The Grammy-winning artiste unveiled the dates for her world tour on Monday, with the initial itinerary including a Lagos concert scheduled for December 22, alongside stops across Europe, North America and South Africa. However, the announcement sparked heated reactions on Nigerian social media, where several users questioned the decision to host the singer amid reports of fresh xenophobic violence targeting Nigerians in South Africa. The controversy revived long-standing tensions between both countries, with some social media users calling for a boycott of the Lagos concert. Others argued that entertainment should not be linked to diplomatic disputes and maintained that musicians should not be held responsible for political or societal conflicts. A number of public figures also weighed in on the debate. Media personality Do2dtun questioned the promoters behind the planned Lagos show, while activist and former presidential candidate Omoyele Sowore urged Nigerians to channel their frustrations toward political leaders rather than the artiste. Neither Tyla nor her management publicly addressed the criticism. However, checks by VANGUARD showed that Lagos has been removed from the list of tour venues on the official ticketing platform. The previously announced December 22 show in Nigeria no longer appears among the available dates. The updated schedule now lists only the remaining international stops, including performances across Europe, North America and two South African shows in Cape Town on January 4 and Johannesburg on January 9. Tyla has not announced whether the Lagos concert was cancelled permanently or if it could be rescheduled at a later date. The post Tyla removes Lagos from world tour after backlash appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Beyond Surgery: Can nutrition and lifestyle help prevent uterine fibroids?
items.description: By Vivian Obi For millions of Nigerian women, prevention may be the missing conversation. This article is adapted from the author’s Master of Public Health capstone research completed at Monroe University, New York. For many Nigerian women, the word fibroid carries more fear than hope. It is a diagnosis often whispered among friends, discussed quietly within families, or discovered unexpectedly after years of enduring painful menstrual periods, heavy bleeding, persistent pelvic pain, or difficulty conceiving. By the time many women seek medical attention, surgery has become the only option presented to them. Across Nigeria, stories of women postponing weddings, delaying pregnancy, struggling with infertility, or travelling long distances in search of treatment have become increasingly common. Families organise fundraisers for surgery. Religious gatherings hold special prayers for women hoping to conceive after a myomectomy. Some women live with symptoms for years because they believe the pain is “normal,” while others avoid hospitals out of fear that they would be told their womb must be removed. These stories are not isolated experiences. They represent a growing public health concern that deserves far more attention than it currently receives. Yet, amid the conversations about surgery and fertility, an equally important question is often overlooked: Can some cases of uterine fibroids be prevented—or at least delayed—through healthier nutrition and lifestyle choices? Recent scientific evidence suggests that the answer may be more encouraging than many people realise. While nutrition and lifestyle cannot completely eliminate the risk of fibroids—and they are certainly not cures—they are increasingly recognised as important factors that may influence how fibroids develop, how quickly they grow, and how severe their symptoms become. This emerging evidence offers women, healthcare professionals, and policymakers an opportunity to shift part of the conversation from treatment alone to prevention and early intervention.A Silent Burden Affecting MillionsUterine fibroids, medically known as leiomyomas, are non-cancerous growths that develop within or around the muscular wall of the uterus. Although they are benign, their impact on women’s health can be profound. Scientific studies estimate that between 70 and 80 percent of women will develop uterine fibroids during their reproductive years, making them the most common non-cancerous tumour affecting women worldwide. Many women never develop symptoms, but for countless others, fibroids become a source of chronic pain, heavy menstrual bleeding, anaemia, recurrent miscarriages, infertility, pregnancy complications, and emotional distress. In many parts of Nigeria, these symptoms are often accepted as a normal part of womanhood. A teenage girl who experiences extremely heavy menstrual bleeding may simply be told that she “takes after her mother.” A newly married woman who struggles to conceive may face blame from family members before anyone considers investigating a possible fibroid. Women suffering persistent pelvic discomfort frequently self-medicate or seek traditional remedies long before consulting a qualified healthcare provider. These delays often mean that fibroids continue growing unnoticed until they significantly affect quality of life. Beyond the physical symptoms lies another burden that receives far less attention—the emotional and financial cost. Women living with fibroids may repeatedly miss work because of severe menstrual bleeding or debilitating pain. Others spend years moving from one hospital to another searching for affordable treatment. Families often shoulder enormous healthcare expenses while coping with anxiety surrounding fertility and future pregnancies. Although much of the available economic research comes from the United States, where fibroids are estimated to cost more than 34 billion dollars annually in healthcare expenses and lost productivity, the financial impact in countries like Nigeria may be even more devastating because most healthcare costs are paid directly by patients and their families. Why Black Women Face Greater Risk One of the most important—and perhaps least understood—findings from recent scientific research is that uterine fibroids do not affect all women equally. Studies consistently show that Black women develop fibroids more frequently, at younger ages, and often experience larger tumours and more severe symptoms than women from many other racial groups. They are also more likely to require surgical treatment during their reproductive years. Scientists believe this disparity results from a complex interaction of genetics, hormones, environmental exposures, vitamin D deficiency, healthcare access, and social determinants of health rather than any single cause. For Nigeria, these findings carry enormous significance. With one of Africa’s largest populations of women of reproductive age, Nigeria may already bear a substantial share of the global burden of uterine fibroids. Yet awareness remains relatively low, preventive education is limited, and many women first learn about fibroids only after symptoms become severe enough to require medical intervention. This reality presents an opportunity for public health leaders. Instead of focusing almost exclusively on surgery after fibroids have developed, greater attention can be given to helping women understand the lifestyle and nutritional factors that research suggests may influence risk before serious complications occur. Importantly, this approach does not imply that women are responsible for causing fibroids. Many risk factors—including age, genetics, and hormonal influences—cannot be changed. However, growing scientific evidence indicates that several lifestyle behaviours are modifiable and may contribute to reducing risk or slowing disease progression.Changing the Conversation from Treatment to PreventionFor decades, medical management of fibroids has centred largely on monitoring tumour growth until symptoms become severe enough to justify medication or surgery. While these treatments remain essential, they do little to address the underlying factors that may contribute to fibroid development. Today, researchers around the world are increasingly exploring a different question: What if prevention began long before surgery became necessary? Emerging evidence suggests that nutrition, vitamin D status, body weight, physical activity, stress management, and environmental exposures may all play meaningful roles in fibroid development. Although researchers continue to study these relationships, the findings already point toward an important public health message: healthy lifestyle choices may not only improve overall wellbeing but could also become valuable tools in reducing the burden of uterine fibroids. For Nigerian women, this shift in thinking could transform how fibroids are discussed—not simply as a condition to be treated after diagnosis, but as a women’s health issue that deserves earlier education, preventive action, and greater national attention. Vivian Obi, MPH, is a public health researcher and graduate of Monroe University, New York. Her work focuses on women’s health, epidemiology, nutrition, disease prevention, and health equity, particularly in African populations. The post Beyond Surgery: Can nutrition and lifestyle help prevent uterine fibroids? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké « Borom Mbary » : un homme de la terre et de savoir
items.description: Sixième enfant de Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, Cheikh Ibrahima « Borom Mbary » n’a certes pas occupé le khalifat. Cependant, son souvenir reste dans le cœur des mourides pour avoir contribué à tous les chantiers de Touba, particulièrement à la construction de la Grande mosquée, mais également pour avoir érigé des « daaras ». Le travail de la terre et l’enseignement coranique rythmaient sa vie. Tout comme son frère aîné, Serigne Abdoullahi Mbacké « Borom Deur Bi », Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké « Borom Mbary » a du sang chérifien par sa mère, venue de la Mauritanie. Ce sixième enfant du fondateur du Mouridisme, né en 1912, n’a pas non plus occupé le khalifat. Surnommé « Borom Mbary » par les fidèles du fait de ses longs séjours et retraites spirituelles à Mbacké Barry, il était un adepte de la terre comme son frère aîné. « Il pratiquait l’agriculture à Daroul Khadim, à l’ouest de Touba », confie Serigne Cheikh Abdou Mbacké, porte-parole de la famille. Toutefois, la notoriété de Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké réside dans son érudition et surtout son rôle de maître coranique et de bâtisseur de « daaras ». « Il a créé plusieurs daaras », selon notre interlocuteur. A lire aussi : Les Baay Faal et leurs accessoires sacrés : voyage au cœur d’un héritage mystique (1/2) Cet engagement pour l’enseignement religieux témoigne d’un riche cursus entamé très tôt auprès de son père. En fait, d’après le récit du porte-parole de la famille, après les enseignements reçus à Diourbel, Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké a été initié au Coran par son « vénéré » père à Diourbel. Il a été ensuite confié au maître de la famille, Serigne Abdourahmane Lô Ndame, chargé d’enrichir son apprentissage. « Après qu’il eut mémorisé le Coran au bout de trois ans et appris la calligraphie, l'illustre marabout de Ndame Lô l’a ramené à Diourbel, auprès de son père », renseigne le porte-parole. Mais, désireux de faire de son enfant un érudit, Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba a encore renvoyé celui-ci auprès de son maître pour parfaire ses connaissances islamiques. Ce nouveau périple pour la quête du savoir a conduit Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké à Kaël (situé dans l’actuel département de Mbacké) et en Mauritanie. Ce parcours initiatique a fini de faire de lui un puits de savoir qu’il a décidé de léguer aux plus jeunes, car pour le maître coranique, l’éducation est capitale pour préserver les jeunes contre certaines tares sociétales. Une générosité légendaire Sur le plan moral, Serigne Cheikh Abdou Mbacké décrit Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké comme un homme « profondément pieux, calme et d’une sérénité absolue ». « Sa générosité était connue de tous. Il partageait ses biens, mais aussi son savoir avec tous ceux qui le sollicitaient pour un conseil ou un appui », confie notre interlocuteur qui admire l’engagement « sans faille » du défunt envers la communauté mouride. D’après lui, il était un fervent défenseur de la communauté mouride et surtout de ses dignitaires à qui il vouait énormément de respect. « L’engagement citoyen » de Serigne Ibrahima Mbacké est également salué par le porte-parole qui renseigne que le guide a toujours contribué aux différents chantiers de Touba. Ainsi, sa contribution majeure et active à la construction de la Grande mosquée de Touba continue de marquer les esprits. Tout comme ses élogieux « xassidas » (poèmes) dédiés à son père, Cheikhoul Khadim, et au maître de la famille, Serigne Abdourahmane Lô Ndame. Une manière d’exprimer sa gratitude à l’endroit des deux grands hommes qui l’ont façonné. Rappelé à Dieu le 21 janvier 1954, Cheikh Ibrahima Mbacké « Borom Mbary » laisse un legs perpétué par le khalife de la famille, Serigne Fallou Mbacké. Fatou SY

items.title: L’afflux massif de Marocains à Ceuta lié au rapprochement entre l’Algérie et l’Espagne ?
items.description: L’évasion de milliers de Marocains vers l’enclave espagnole de Ceuta suscite des interrogations sur l’implication du Maroc dans un nouveau chantage migratoire envers l’Espagne et l’Union européenne. Si en Europe, la droite et l’extrême droite prennent pour cible le gouvernement espagnol de Pedro Sanchez pour sa politique migratoire, un expert allemand des questions migratoires estime plausible l'existence d'un probable lien avec le récent rapprochement entre Madrid et Alger. Interrogé par le site 20minutes.ch , Benjamin Schraven, expert en migration au sein de l'Institut allemand de développement et de durabilité (IDOS), à Bonn, juge l’hypothèse crédible. « C'est plausible. L'Espagne et l'Algérie se sont de nouveau rapprochées sur la question du Sahara occidental. L'Algérie soutient le Polisario, qui lutte pour l'indépendance du Sahara occidental. On peut donc supposer que le Maroc pourrait signaler à l’Espagne : si vous vous rapprochez trop de l'Algérie, nous pouvons aussi réagir. Il n'y a cependant aucune preuve à ce jour », a-t-il répondu à la question de savoir si la fuite massive de Marocains vers Ceuta est liée au rapprochement entre l’Algérie et l’Espagne. La coïncidence est troublante. Crise de Ceuta : le Maroc cherche-t-il à punir l’Espagne pour son rapprochement avec l’Algérie ? Curieusement, le Maroc a lâché sa bombe migratoire, une semaine après la visite du chef du gouvernement espagnol Pedro Sanchez à Alger, lundi 20 juillet. De retour en Espagne, M. Sanchez a qualifié cette visite de « tournant » dans les relations algéro-espagnoles qui ont connu une grave crise en 2022 à la suite de la décision de Madrid de s’aligner sur les thèses marocaines concernant le Sahara occidental. Ce changement de position est survenu après la crise moratoire de mai 2021, quand le Maroc a ouvert ses frontières à plus de 10.000 migrants pour prendre d’assaut Ceuta. Ce précédent crédite la thèse d’un nouveau chantage migratoire de Rabat contre Madrid, évoqué également par la presse espagnole. « Les relations avec le Maroc sont excellentes et ne sont aucunement affectées par les bonnes relations avec l’Algérie », ont indiqué à Europa Press des sources du ministère des Affaires étrangères espagnol. Toutefois, il est difficile de comprendre comment plus de 50.000 Marocains ont pu traverser aussi facilement la frontière avec Ceuta dans un pays où le Makhzen (administration parallèle) exerce un contrôle strict sur la population. Le journal espagnol spécialiste du Maghreb, Ignacio Cembrero, évoque un autre motif : la pression migratoire sur Ceuta sert au Maroc pour « relancer ses revendications sur la ville. » Pedro Sanchez dénonce une atteinte à l’intégrité territoriale de l’Espagne En plus du rapprochement entre Alger et Madrid et des revendications marocaines sur Ceuta et Melilla, d’autres sources évoquent une probable implication d’Israël dans l’afflux massif de migrants marocains. Le ministre iranien des Affaires étrangères Abbas Araghchi a accusé le Premier ministre israélien Benjamin Netanyahu et le président américain Donald Trump d’utiliser le Maroc pour punir l’Espagne à cause de son soutien à la Palestine. « Le régime marocain n'est qu'un autre outil de Netanyahu et Trump. Ils punissent l'Espagne pour son soutien à la Palestine », a-t-il écrit vendredi sur la plateforme X. Pour Pedro Sanchez, dont le gouvernement a ménagé le Maroc, l’afflux massif de Marocains à Ceuta est une atteinte à « l'intégrité territoriale de l'Espagne. » L’article L'afflux massif de Marocains à Ceuta lié au rapprochement entre l'Algérie et l'Espagne ? est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: L’armée russe frappe à Kiev des usines produisant des composants pour missiles et drones (VIDEOS)
items.description: Les forces russes ont frappe dans la nuit du 31 juillet au 1er août l'usine Fire Point de Kiev, qui fabrique des composants et des charges utiles pour les missiles de croisiere Flamingo, a indique le ministere russe de la Defense dans son communique. Parmi les usines touchees dans la capitale ukrainienne figurent egalement une entreprise du secteur de l'electronique et de la radiotransmission Radioizmeritel, ou etaient produites des pieces pour les drones FP-1 et les missiles Neptune-MD ainsi que l'usine d'assemblage electronique Bourevestnik, charge de la fabrication de composants pour les drones et les equipements radar. Russian strikes on Kyiv and air defense activity. POV 50.489652, 30.528595 @GeoConfirmed pic.twitter.com/PHNSPS88KM — 3BM15 (@3_bm15) August 1, 2026 La Defense russe annonce avoir frappe l'entreprise industrielle Kiev-111, qui fabrique des composants et des tetes de frappe pour les missiles ailes a lancement terrestre FP-5, et l'entreprise industrielle Kiev-25, qui assure la production et le stockage des equipements logiciels et materiels destines aux systemes de guerre electronique Lima. Le site d'assemblage et de stockage de drones Kiev-21 a egalement ete cible. Dans la region de Kiev, le centre logistique de Vichnevoïe, ou etaient stockes et assembles des composants pour drones, a ete touche, tandis que dans la region d'Odessa, deux navires transportant du materiel militaire ont ete frappes. Footage showing the moment of the Russian Iskander-M/Zircon missile strikes near the CHP-5 power plant in Kyiv. The power plant itself does not appear to have been the target, but rather some industrial zone nearby. https://t.co/Xn1xMw57nv pic.twitter.com/nynmAwtZNx — AMK Mapping 🇳🇿 (@AMK_Mapping_) July 31, 2026 Les forces russes ont attaque ces cibles a l'aide d'armes de haute precision basees a terre et en mer, ainsi qu'a l'aide de drones. Zelensky a declare que le systeme de defense antiaerienne ukrainien n'avait reussi a abattre qu'un seul missile balistique la nuit derniere et s'est plaint du manque de missiles intercepteurs. Le ministere russe de la Defense a souligne a plusieurs reprises que l'armee russe frappe les infrastructures militaires et industrielles afin de reduire le potentiel militaro-economique de l'adversaire. Pour ce faire, elle utilise des drones d'attaque et des armes de haute precision a longue portee, capables de detruire n'importe quelle cible, tant a Kiev que sur l'ensemble du territoire ukrainien.

items.title: 2Baba: Annie still in love?
items.description: …Likes ex-hubby’s post amid reconciliation denials By Tony-Okafor Favour Annie Idibia may have said there’s no reunion, but her actions are telling a different story. Days after debunking viral videos that suggested a possible reconciliation with ex-husband 2Baba, the actress has reignited speculation by liking one of the singer’s latest posts on Instagram. The post, shared by 2Baba’s manager Mallam Yankere, showed the music icon in motion with him on the road. Annie was among the first 793 people to like the photo.. Fans quickly spotted it. “Annie just liked this post o. @official2baba #@annieidibia are soul mates,” IG user Faith Dewodo @faith_enyonama wrote. Digital creator, Elizabeth Rukky @elizabethrukky_ also commented: “Annie liked this post. Wow.” The buzz comes just days after Annie addressed rumours of a reunion. She clarified that a viral clip making rounds online was old and did not mean she and 2Baba were getting back together. According to her, she is currently focused on raising her daughters and growing her career. 2Baba also shut down the rumours on his Instagram Story, writing,”Abeg na old video o” The former couple went through years of public marital challenges before their union officially ended in early 2025. 2Baba confirmed the separation and has since remarried. Annie, on her part, says she is still single. Despite both moving on, the viral clip and Annie’s latest Instagram activity have once again sparked conversations about their past and whether a reconciliation is possible. With both stars now making it clear there is”no going back”, the July 26 like has done little to stop fans from hoping. For many, the message is simple: the marriage may be over, but the love story isn’t forgotten. The post 2Baba: Annie still in love? appeared first on Vanguard News .
