items.title: FIFA scraps private investment plan after backlash
items.description: FIFA president Gianni Infantino said on Saturday he has scrapped a plan to allow private investment in the World Cup following fierce backlash from football officials worldwide. “Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve,” Infantino said in a statement. “As a result, this proposal will not proceed.” FIFA, world football’s governing body, had floated the plan on Tuesday, saying it could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for a new FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a commercial subsidiary it proposed to run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup. It said that, if approved, the project could provide each of FIFA’s 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027 and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million. The Asian Football Confederation, which represents 47 member nations, welcomed the plan’s withdrawal on Saturday. Any initiative that may impact global football should be “presented and discussed with the Confederations, the FIFA Council, Member Associations (MAs) and other stakeholders in a timely, transparent and meaningful manner,” the Kuala Lumpur-based body said in a statement. The Mexican Football Federation also welcomed the move, saying that “unity among all the Confederations and Federations has been prioritised for the good of football”. Earlier this week, European football’s governing body UEFA said none of its national teams would participate in any FIFA competition “for so long as these proposals remain alive”. The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and North American and Caribbean federation (CONCACAF) also condemned the move. “The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product,” UEFA said in a statement. “No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.” Pressure mounted on Infantino on Friday with the resignation of senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro, who called the idea “a bad deal for FIFA’s member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game”. South American confederation CONMEBOL, whose president Alejandro Dominguez is regarded as a close ally of Infantino, demanded further information on the “scope, structure, governance and potential effects” of the project. – ‘Created divisions’ – In the late-night statement announcing the plan was dead, Infantino said the project was conceived as a means of strengthening member associations, and that it would only have gone ahead if a majority supported it. “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place,” he said. FIFA had tried to fend off the critics, saying in a statement early Friday that it would continue consultations with member associations and insisting that “nobody is selling football”. But the pressure mounted, and not just within the football community. A day after the European Union praised UEFA for “defending the integrity of the game,” UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that Infantino was “the wrong man” to lead FIFA. The beleaguered Infantino said he would focus now on restoring harmony while continuing to grow the game. “Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support,” he said. AFP The post FIFA scraps private investment plan after backlash appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: En diabolisant l’Algérie, on dessert les intérêts de la Tunisie
items.description: Suite à l’article publié dans votre journal et intitulé ‘‘Les menaces réelles de la stabilité tunisienne’’ de M. Elyes Kasri, je ne peux, en tant que citoyen algérien profondément attaché à l’axe Tunis- Alger, rester silencieux face à des accusations aussi graves portées contre l’Algérie. En tant que fervent partisan des relations algéro-tunisiennes, j’ai souhaité apporter un éclairage factuel, juridique et historique afin de déconstruire certaines approximations qui nuisent à une analyse sereine de la géopolitique de notre région. Dr Abderrahmane Cherfouh * Qu’un ancien ambassadeur, ayant exercé les plus hautes fonctions de représentation de l’État tunisien à l'étranger, se prête à un tel pamphlet à charge est particulièrement regrettable. Une lecture lucide des relations tuniso-algériennes Face à la récurrence d’analyses à charge tendant à ériger l’Algérie en menace pour la Tunisie, et à un discours nourri de contrevérités, d’approximations historiques, économiques et juridiques, il apparaît indispensable de rétablir les faits. L’auteur de l’article porte, une fois de plus, des accusations particulièrement graves contre le voisin algérien. Habitué des réquisitoires à charge, il s’appuie malheureusement sur des contresens historiques et des approximations géopolitiques qui masquent les réalités de notre région. Il me paraît indispensable de substituer l’émotion à la rigueur des faits, des traités et de notre histoire commune. Au-delà des postures individuelles, la responsabilité impose le respect des faits, du droit international et des engagements qui unissent nos deux nations. 1. Frontières terrestres – Un cadre juridique définitif et incontestable : affirmer que l’Algérie occupe des territoires tunisiens relève d’une méconnaissance flagrante du droit international. Les frontières terrestres entre nos deux pays ne souffrent d’aucune ambiguïté. Elles ont été définitivement délimitées par l’accord du 20 mars 1970, puis consolidées par la convention du 19 mars 1983. Ce cadre juridique bilatéral a définitivement réglé les contentieux hérités de la période coloniale. Agiter aujourd’hui le spectre d’une prétendue spoliation territoriale constitue un anachronisme qui ne repose sur aucune réalité juridique. 2. Sécurité énergétique – L’Algérie, partenaire constant et non prédateur : accuser l’Algérie de nuire à la Tunisie sur le plan énergétique est un non-sens économique. C'est exactement l’inverse qui se produit. Grâce au gazoduc TransMed, l’Algérie fournit entre 65 % et 70 % du gaz naturel indispensable à la production d’électricité tunisienne. Ce partenariat stratégique, assorti de facilités de paiement durant les périodes de difficultés macroéconomiques, constitue le véritable poumon énergétique de la Tunisie. On ne cherche pas à déstabiliser un pays que l’on contribue quotidiennement à alimenter en énergie. En géopolitique, les intentions réelles ne se mesurent pas aux rumeurs, mais aux flux économiques. Fragiliser l’axe énergétique Alger-Tunis ne pénaliserait pas l’Algérie : cela infligerait une double peine à l’économie et aux consommateurs tunisiens. Les menaces réelles à la stabilité tunisienne 3. Stress hydrique – L’impératif de la coopération face au changement climatique : imputer le stress hydrique tunisien à une prétendue volonté d’assèchement de ses ressources de la part de l'Algérie relève d’une aberration scientifique. L’ensemble du Maghreb subit les conséquences du changement climatique. Bien loin de s’opposer sur cette ressource vitale, l’Algérie, la Tunisie et la Libye ont signé à Tripoli un accord historique visant à mettre en place un mécanisme commun de gestion des eaux souterraines du Système aquifère du Sahara septentrional. Cet accord garantit un échange transparent de données et une exploitation équitable des ressources. Si l’on suivait le raisonnement développé dans cet article, il faudrait croire que l’Algérie consacrerait ses journées à assécher les nappes phréatiques communes tout en subventionnant le gaz qui éclaire les foyers tunisiens. Une telle contradiction ne résiste pas une seconde à l’épreuve des faits. 4. Flux transnationaux – Ne pas confondre crises subies et manœuvres politiques : réduire les phénomènes de contrebande et les flux migratoires subsahariens à de prétendues manœuvres algériennes constitue un raccourci simpliste. La contrebande frontalière pénalise d’abord l’économie algérienne, en détournant massivement des produits fortement subventionnés par l’État, notamment les carburants et les produits alimentaires. Quant à la crise migratoire, elle est continentale. Avec des milliers de kilomètres de frontières sahéliennes, l’Algérie en subit les effets au même titre que la Tunisie. Présenter cette réalité comme une stratégie de déstabilisation revient à occulter le rôle des réseaux criminels de passeurs ainsi que les insuffisances des politiques migratoires européennes. 5. Vérités historiques – Gafsa et la lutte contre le terrorisme : l’exercice de désinformation atteint son paroxysme lorsque l’auteur tente de réécrire l’histoire en attribuant à l'Algérie les événements tragiques de Gafsa en 1980. Les archives historiques établissent clairement que cette agression contre la Tunisie du Président Habib Bourguiba fut organisée par le régime libyen de l’époque. L’Algérie s’y était opposée **. De la même manière, suggérer une quelconque complaisance de l’Algérie envers le terrorisme constitue une insulte à la mémoire de toute la région. L’Algérie a payé un tribut humain considérable durant la décennie noire pour éradiquer ce fléau. Forte de cette expérience douloureuse, elle constitue aujourd’hui un partenaire essentiel de la Tunisie dans la lutte contre le terrorisme, grâce à un échange permanent de renseignements et à une coopération opérationnelle le long de la frontière commune. Notre destin commun face aux défis du siècle La doctrine de sécurité nationale algérienne repose sur un principe simple : une Tunisie instable constitue une menace directe pour la sécurité de l’Algérie. Alger n’a donc aucun intérêt politique, économique ou sécuritaire à fragiliser Tunis. L’amitié algéro-tunisienne n’est ni un slogan ni une formule diplomatique. Elle est une réalité géographique, historique et humaine, scellée notamment par le sang versé à Sakiet Sidi Youssef. On ne badine pas avec la mémoire des martyrs. Prétendre que l’Algérie entretient un lien avec le terrorisme revient à insulter la mémoire des militaires algériens et tunisiens tombés sous les mêmes balles, notamment dans le massif du Chaambi. La sécurité frontalière n’est pas une faveur : elle est notre tranchée commune. Diviser pour régner demeure une vieille recette coloniale. À qui profiterait une discorde durable entre Alger et Tunis ? Certainement pas à nos deux peuples. Fragiliser notre voisinage immédiat, c’est ouvrir la porte aux ingérences étrangères qui rêvent de transformer le Maghreb en terrain de rivalités géopolitiques. Enfin, l’auteur pousse le contresens diplomatique jusqu’à accuser l’Algérie d’exercer un prétendu chantage énergétique ou terroriste afin d’isoler la Tunisie sur la scène internationale. Comment peut-on sérieusement prêter à Alger la volonté d’isoler un pays dont elle défend régulièrement les intérêts dans les enceintes internationales, rappelant constamment que la stabilité de la Tunisie constitue une condition essentielle de la sécurité régionale ? Qu’un ancien ambassadeur, censé incarner la retenue, la nuance et le sens de l’État, se laisse aller à des accusations gratuites est profondément regrettable. La diplomatie n’est ni le lieu des ressentiments personnels ni celui des invectives. Elle exige de la hauteur de vue. En cherchant à diaboliser le partenaire algérien, l’auteur ne fragilise pas l’Algérie ; il affaiblit sa propre crédibilité et dessert les intérêts stratégiques profonds de la Tunisie. * Médecin algérien résident au Canada. ** L'implication d'éléments de l'armée algérienne dans l'organisation de cette attaque de Gafsa a été prouvée et documentée par des historiens (NDLR). Tunisie-Algérie | Les graines de la discorde L’article En diabolisant l’Algérie, on dessert les intérêts de la Tunisie est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Blood on Oghara Farm Road: Delta’s kidnap kingdom, where trip to harvest cassava could cost your life
items.description: By Paul Olayemi, Oghara The cassava the couple spent the previous morning cultivating was still scattered along the bush path when Mrs Adojor learnt her husband, Vincent Adojor, was dead. Read Also: New Army Divisions: Veterans split over timeline, funding fears It was neither from a phone call nor from a policeman at her door but, from a neighbour who came to see her in the hospital. She had spent the whole night in captivity believing the man she farmed beside the day earlier was simply “receiving treatment somewhere.” He wasn’t. He had been shot on the walk home, on a path they had taken a thousand times with baskets, sacks and sometimes buckets full of yam, corn, cassava, and okra in the past. “I never knew my husband was dead. I thought he had only been shot and was receiving treatment in a hospital,” she says. Her voice worn thin by grief as she spoke to Saturday Vanguard The day her husband was shot, the captors brutalized and shoved her further into the bush. To them, one shot meant nothing. This is Oghara today: a kingdom old enough to be remembered as the historic “Gateway to Urhobo land,” home to a state’s Teaching Hospital and Polytechnic, a Naval Base and a base for a Police Mobile Force Unit, oil and gas installations dotting its edges — and, running quietly through the middle of it all, a farm road that residents have learned to fear. A Kingdom Under Siege Ask anyone in Oghara, the home town of Chief James Ibori, a former governor of Delta State, what month it happened, and they won’t need to think about it. Leonard Maduku would tell you it was 2024, the year his younger brother never made it home from the farm. Jackson Erifeta would tell you it was Thursday, July 3, 2025 — the day his mother rode her bicycle into an ambush and never rode back out. Evans Gaius remembers 9:30 p.m. on February 28, 2025, the exact minute a dagger found his stomach at his own front gate. Happy Ejorowho remembers the cutlass and the fall of August 15, 2024. Stephen Owotuoma remembers three days in the bush that August that cost him his motorcycle, and, he says, his peace of mind ever since. And Godday Akine remembers a Friday in 2024, when what should have been a routine ride to the farm with his younger brother turned into four days of beatings, threats and captivity in the forest. Ask His Royal Majesty, Noble Oyibo Eshemitan, Orefe III, the Ovie of Oghara Kingdom, and he won’t give you a date at all. He’ll give you a calendar. “Since January to date, every month, it’s become a recurring decimal,” the monarch says, weariness breaking through the formality in his voice. “There’s no month since January to date that we don’t have kidnapping, killing.” By his count, not a single month this year has been spared. January bled. February bled. March, April, May — all of them bled. Then came the killing that finally cracked something open in the kingdom: the Adojor case, the man who was shot dead when returning back from farm while his widow was marched into the bush and held until N1.5 million was scraped together to buy back a life that still needed saving. “They Wear Us Down With the Cutlass” The victims’ accounts start to sound like one long, repeating nightmare with different names stitched onto it. Isaac Oragborfia was kidnapped alongside his wife just three months ago, walking home from the farm. Four men, he says, spoke a language he recognised at once. “They were Northerners, the way they spoke they were Hausas,” he insisted. His phone was taken, N3 million was demanded and eventually paid — raised, in the end, by his own son, who carried the ransom into the bush himself to buy his parents’ freedom. “They kept beating us all through,” he said. “Since then, I have not been doing anything.” Happy Ejorowho was carrying cassava home from the farm when five men fell on him. “A tall guy… he was the one carrying cutlass. He used the cutlass to hit me and I fell,” he recalls. In the bush, he found he wasn’t alone — two others had already been taken before him. Each of them paid N2 million to get out. He drives a fairly used motorcycle for a living now; the farm isn’t somewhere he trusts anymore. Ruth Owotuoma didn’t stay to negotiate. Attacked on her bicycle at 4 p.m. one afternoon last June by two men she describes as unmistakably Hausa, she ran — and paid for that decision with weeks in the teaching hospital, recovering from what the escape cost her. Esther Alubu wasn’t as fortunate. She was riding to the farm with her son when gunfire cracked ahead of them; she turned back, but too late. Two men she describes as Fulani threw wood across her path, dragged her and another woman into the bush, and marched them through a night of rain until ransoms of N1.5 million and N2 million, respectively, bought their release the following morning. Then there’s Godday Akine, ambushed with his younger brother shortly after 6 a.m. on a Friday in 2024, at a waterlogged stretch of farm road where their motorcycle had to slow down. One man stepped into their path; another struck Akine across the head with a piece of wood, hard enough to put him on the ground. When his brother tried to run, one of the attackers caught him near the eye. Four kidnappers in all overpowered them, dragged them into the bush, bound them, beat them, and warned them that shouting would get them shot. Using the brother’s phone, the kidnappers called the family themselves to open ransom talks. The brothers spent four days in the forest before their captors settled on a price — N1 million each, plus N600,000 for “food” — later negotiated down to N2.3 million total. They were released around 10 p.m., taken straight to a private Hospital, where Akine’s head wound was stitched and his eye treated. Neighbours pooled money for the hospital bill; some borrowed what they didn’t have. The wound has since closed. What hasn’t closed is Akine’s relationship with the farm that nearly killed him. And then there’s Godstime Agent, whose wife’s story ends the way no one prayed for — a corpse found. “We now saw her corpse in the bush,” he says, still unable, weeks later, to bring himself to bury her. “She was brutally—” he breaks down in tears. He doesn’t finish the sentence. He doesn’t need to. The Mother Who Wouldn’t Stop Fighting Them Jackson Erifeta buried his father in March 2025. Four months later, in July, he buried his mother too. She’d gone to the farm on a Thursday, cycling alongside colleagues on motorcycles. She never came home. By the next morning, after a frantic overnight search, her family found her body where she’d fallen. “There were signs that she had been attacked,” Jackson says. “It appeared the assailants had tried to cut her, but when they could not overpower her, they used her own clothing to strangle her to death.” What haunts him isn’t just how she died — it’s how many warnings went unheeded before it happened. “My mother had repeatedly complained about some Fulani herdsmen who were rearing cattle in the area,” he says. “She often complained that they were disturbing her and other farmers. She had told us that whenever she asked them to leave the farm, they would threaten her.” She kept confronting them anyway. It was, her son believes now, a fight that cost her everything. “July has become a very painful month for me,” he says, “because it reminds me of her death.” A Kingdom That Buries and Buries Again For Leonard Maduku, there was no ransom call to answer — only silence, and then a body. His brother, Abraham Edesiri Maduku, vanished from the farm in 2024. Two days passed with no ransom demand, so the family went looking themselves. They found his bicycle first. His body soon after. “We reported it at the police station,” Leonard says, “and their response was that they would look into the matter. But from that time until now, there has been no confrontation with anyone.” He and his family now raise his brother’s four children — three boys and a girl — paying school fees for a man who no longer can. Igho Adojor, daughter of the murdered Vincent Adojor, remembers being lied to for her own protection. She called home again and again, desperate for news of her mother, while relatives shielded her from the truth that her father was already gone. “We were devastated,” she says simply. “All we could do was cry.” Her father had held the family together — farmer, businessman, provider for two wives and ten children, the eldest of whom is at Delta State University. “Now that he has been killed, we do not know how we will survive.” Her mother isn’t asking for sympathy. She’s asking for help. “I have seven children,” she says. “How do I train them? The government should help me.” When Ransom Becomes a Shopping List Nothing captures the cold, transactional nature of this crisis quite like the list Mrs Adojor was made to fill while negotiating for her own freedom: a large loaf of bread, five tins of sardine, five tins of milk, two packets of Benson cigarettes, wraps of weed, Tramadol tablets, a crate of malt drink, sachets of water. A kidnappers’ care package, itemised and delivered, before a single naira of ransom changed hands. Even talking to her captors was a struggle. Unable to understand their language, the women had to track down a Hausa woman at Oghara’s cattle market to interpret the negotiations by phone — a woman who initially refused, and agreed only after they pleaded with her. “An Isolated Case,” said the Commissioner If one line has enraged Oghara more than any other in recent weeks, it’s this: the Delta State Commissioner of Police, CP Yemi (Olufemi) Oyeniyi, meeting the monarch, chiefs and community stakeholders at the palace after Mr Adojor’s killing, promised strengthened, intelligence-led policing — then described what Oghara is living through as amounting to only “some isolated cases of kidnapping and cultism.” The Oghara Study Group wasn’t willing to let that stand. In a statement issued shortly after the commissioner’s visit, the group said it welcomed the engagement but flatly rejected the framing, insisting the kingdom is facing “an organised and persistent kidnapping crisis,” not scattered, unrelated incidents. Its own documentation, the group said, shows a recurring pattern of abductions, killings and multimillion-naira ransom payments running the length of the Oghara–Sapele, Otefe–Ovade and Warri–Sapele corridors — hardly the footprint of anything “isolated.” High Chief Stephen Egbivwie, the Unugbrogodo — traditional prime minister, clan head, and head of the council of chiefs — of Ogharefe in Oghara Kingdom, said, “That Commissioner of Police should describe what we face as an isolated case — that is not proper. We have asked the cattle rearers to leave our bushes, leave our farms. They attack our people, kill many, and kidnap many for ransom of millions of naira.” Asked for the police’s position on the “isolated case” remark and the broader pattern of attacks, force spokesman Edafe Bright pointed to action taken rather than disputing the numbers. “As a follow-up to these reported incidents, the CP personally visited Oghara late June, met with the king, stakeholders, the chairman of Ethiope West LGA, vigilantes and other stakeholders, deliberated and modalities were put in place,” he said. “And I think from that time till now, we have not recorded any other incidents.” The Chairman Who Won’t Answer His Phone While the king speaks, while the chiefs speak, while grieving mothers and widowed fathers speak, one man has stayed conspicuously silent: Hon. Christian Onogba, Chairman of Ethiope West Local Government Council. Repeated visits to his secretariat, repeated calls, repeated texts — all unanswered, from the man whose council sits at the administrative centre of a kingdom now burying its own on what feels like a monthly schedule. Beyond the spokesman’s account of the late-June meeting and its “modalities,” the police have offered little else: no arrest figures, no update on the Maduku case or the others still open, just a promise — relayed through the palace — of a rebuilt vigilante network under a newly posted Divisional Police Officer the king describes, carefully, as showing early promise. A Youth Association Running Out of Patience In Obromudu community, under the wider Oghara Kingdom, the Adojor killing is painful — and a warning. “Such an incident has occurred in Obromudu Community,” says Comrade Godstime Agwariame, the community’s youth chairman, flanked by his vice chairman, Comrade Sylvester Abogore, himself the nephew of the murdered man. “Neighbouring communities have experienced several cases of kidnapping.” He recounts the day itself in the flat, practised language of someone who has told this story too many times already: the distress call, the rush to the scene, the crowd already gathered around a lifeless body, the desperate search for the missing wife stretching from that afternoon into a ransom negotiation that opened at N30 million and eventually settled — if “settled” is the word — around N3 million. Even as he speaks, another case is unfolding. “Just yesterday,” he says, “one of our brothers from a neighbouring community reported that his brother had gone to the farm to harvest palm fruits and had been missing for three days. The things he went to the farm with were found there, including his slippers, but there has been no information about his whereabouts up till now.” The youths aren’t waiting on anyone else anymore. Under the Oghara Youth Association, they’ve organised their own watch rotations across the farms, while the traditional council — working from the belief that the attackers are herdsmen operating out of the bush — has ordered cattle owners to bring their animals into town, where they can be watched. The Kingdom’s Reckoning With Itself What makes the king’s account most striking is that he doesn’t let his own kingdom off the hook. Pressed on persistent rumours that some Oghara indigenes have been quietly leasing farmland to herdsmen — land that then becomes staging ground for this very violence — the monarch doesn’t deny it. He confirms it. “We had that information,” he says. “Seven of them were brought to this palace… just because they want to get money. We warned them, and they owned up that they no longer give our land to cattle rearers.” The kingdom’s chiefs, he says, have now resolved collectively: no more land to herdsmen, on pain of banishment. It’s an uncomfortable thing to admit publicly. He could easily have said nothing at all. What Oghara Is Demanding Now The Oghara Study Group has moved well past press statements. The group is preparing to petition the Ethiope West Local Government Legislative Council, the Delta State House of Assembly and the National Assembly for formal public hearings — hearings that would put victims, survivors and security agencies on record together. It’s also exploring strategic public-interest litigation to test, in open court, whether government has met its constitutional duty to protect lives under Section 14(2)(b) of the 1999 Constitution. Its demands are specific: intelligence-led operations against known criminal hideouts, more police personnel and rapid-response vehicles for Ethiope West, a Community Security Liaison Desk at the local government level, better lighting and surveillance along the Oghara–Sapele and Otefe–Ovade corridors, psychosocial support for survivors, and an independent socio-economic impact assessment to finally put a number on what this crisis has cost the kingdom — in ransom, in lost farmland, in disrupted schooling, in shattered households. The group has also drawn a hard line against the unrest that consumed the mosque. “OSG strongly rejects mob justice, vigilantism, ethnic profiling and collective blame,” its brief states. “Criminals must be identified through credible investigations and prosecuted in accordance with the law.” The Long Night That Isn’t Ending For now, Oghara waits — for a new Divisional Police Officer to succeed where his predecessors didn’t, for a local government chairman to finally answer his phone, for a state government to treat the kingdom as something more than an “isolated case.” The police point to the late-June meeting and its aftermath as proof the modalities are working; people on the farm roads say the fear hasn’t caught up with that assessment yet. It waits, too, for something no policy can legislate: the courage of ordinary people to keep walking to their farms. “We are just managing and struggling to survive,” says Igho Adojor, speaking for a family that lost a father, and for a time, a mother, in a single afternoon. “There is no help from anywhere. Only God can help us.” In Oghara today, that isn’t a figure of speech. For many families here, it’s the entire security plan. items.title: Why the Court of Appeal is unable to rule on AG’s stay application
items.description: A newly constituted Court of Appeal panel that sat on an emergency basis Friday morning to hear the Attorney-General’s application for a stay of execution in the Sedina Tamakloe Attionu case has failed to reach a decision, leaving the former MASLOC Chief Executive Officer behind bars as the courts head into a two-month vacation. The panel, made up of Justices Sophia Rosetta Bernasko Essah (presiding), Dr Ernest Owusu-Dapaa and Aryittey Armah-Tetteh, was convened at extremely short notice, with the court itself acknowledging that the respondent’s lawyers had not been properly served. Yet remarkably, the judges retired to write their judgment around 10:20 am, only to return nearly two hours later to announce they could not agree on a ruling. The court has now indicated it will seek a warrant from the Chief Justice to sit during the legal vacation, a move that could leave Ms Tamakloe Attionu at Nsawam Prison for weeks longer, despite her acquittal and discharge by a previous panel just a day earlier. A rushed application, a short-served respondent The timeline of events has raised serious questions about procedural fairness. On Thursday, July 30, the Court of Appeal delivered its unanimous judgment acquitting and discharging Ms Tamakloe Attionu. Hours later, the Attorney-General’s office filed an urgent application for a stay of execution pending an appeal to the Supreme Court. The application was served on the prison authorities in the evening, well after normal court hours, but critically, Ms Tamakloe Attionu’s lawyers were not informed. Her legal team only learned of the application through informal channels and made their way to court Friday morning to find proceedings already being set in motion. “Her lawyer was not informed. But he got wind of it, so he was in court before the judges came in,” a source close to the matter said. The court acknowledged that Ms Tamakloe Attionu had been short-served, a fundamental breach of procedural rules that ordinarily would have warranted an adjournment to allow the respondent to file an affidavit in opposition. However, with Friday being the last day of the legal year, an adjournment would have pushed the matter to October at the earliest. Lawyer waives right to proceed In a move that legal observers say reflects both desperation and duty, Ms Tamakloe Attionu’s lawyer, Mr Enoch Deegbe, waived his right to file an affidavit and proceeded to argue on points of law. This was a significant concession. The rules of procedure exist to ensure both parties have adequate time to prepare and respond. By waiving that right, Mr Deegbe ensured the case could be heard before the vacation, but at the cost of his client’s full opportunity to be heard. “What happened on Friday is deeply concerning from a fairness perspective,” said a private legal practitioner who spoke on condition of anonymity. “A stay of execution application that could keep someone in prison — someone who has already been acquitted — was heard without giving the respondent’s lawyers proper notice, and with the respondent herself not in a position to file any response. That’s not how the justice system should work.” Judges retire — but cannot decide After hearing submissions from both sides, the panel retired to deliberate at around 10:20 am. For nearly two hours, the judges were in chambers. When they returned, the court announced it had been unable to reach a decision. “I can’t believe it,” one court observer was overheard saying. “They sat all this time and couldn’t decide?” The panel then adjourned the matter sine die — indefinitely — and indicated it would apply to the Chief Justice for a warrant to sit during the legal vacation to deliver a ruling. Both parties will be served with hearing notices when a date is fixed. The consequences of delay The practical effect of Friday’s non-decision is that Ms Tamakloe Attionu, who was acquitted and discharged by a unanimous Court of Appeal on Thursday, remains incarcerated at Nsawam Medium Security Female Prison. She was extradited from the United States on June 9, 2026, after being convicted in absentia by the High Court on April 16, 2024, on 78 counts including conspiracy to steal, stealing, causing financial loss to the state, money laundering and procurement-related offences. She had travelled to the US in 2021 with the court’s permission for medical treatment and requested what she referred to as necessary extensions, which at one point the court refused to accommodate and ruled in her absence. She spent 6 months in jail in Nevada before her extradition. The appellate court that acquitted her on Thursday — Justices Emmanuel Ankamah, Emmanuel Senyo Amedahe and Samuel Obeng-Diawuo — found that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. That acquittal, which should have meant immediate release, has now been effectively frozen by the Attorney-General’s application, despite no ruling having been granted. Unanswered questions The proceedings raise difficult questions about the administration of justice in Ghana: · How can a court hear a stay application on an emergency basis when the respondent has not been properly served? · Is it fair for a respondent to be effectively forced to waive their procedural rights simply because the legal year is ending? · Why did a panel of three judges – after nearly two hours of deliberation – fail to reach a decision, leaving the matter unresolved? · Will a warrant during vacation delay matters even further, keeping an acquitted person in custody? . Since the stay of execution has not yet been granted, is it legal to keep a person who has been acquitted and discharged by a court of competent jurisdiction in jail until the court deems it fit to render judgment? What the law says Under Order 79 Rule 1 of C.I. 47, the Chief Justice may appoint any day, including days during vacation, for the hearing of matters. The court has indicated it will apply for such a warrant. However, legal experts note that the granting of a stay of execution pending appeal is not automatic. The test is well-established: the applicant must demonstrate a real likelihood of success on appeal and that irreparable harm would occur if the stay is not granted. The respondent, in turn, has a right to be heard. Whether those standards were properly met in Friday’s proceedings – where the respondent was short-served and unable to file an affidavit – remains an open question. The issue also hovers about whether a judgment of a Court of Appeal in a criminal matter acquitting and discharging the accused can be subjected to a stay of execution, seeing that it is a declaratory judgment and not an executory order. Looking ahead The Chief Justice is expected to rule on the panel’s request for a warrant to sit during vacation in the coming days. If granted, the panel will reconvene to deliver its ruling on the stay application. If the stay is granted, Ms Tamakloe Attionu will remain in custody pending the Supreme Court’s determination of the substantive appeal — a process that could take months or years. If the stay is refused, she will be released immediately. For now, Ms Tamakloe Attionu, who spent weeks at the BNI cells and Police Hospital under guard, and has already spent more than a month at Nsawam Prison and was acquitted just a day ago, remains behind bars, caught in a procedural limbo that has left many questioning whether justice is truly being served.

items.title: Voyage en Algérie : voici comment déclarer ses devises et objets de valeur
items.description: Avec la plateforme numérique Algerian Customs Electronic System (ALCES) des Douanes algériennes, les voyageurs au départ et à destination de l'Algérie, peuvent désormais déclarer leurs devises et objets de valeur en ligne, avant de se rendre à l’aéroport ou au port. Lancé le 1er juin 2025, le système ALCES était jusqu'à présent réservé aux professionnels du commerce extérieur, notamment aux commissionnaires en douane et aux entreprises effectuant des opérations d'importation et d'exportation. Voyage en Algérie : comment effectuer les formalités douanières en ligne Depuis le 25 juillet 2026, son utilisation a été étendue aux particuliers. Les voyageurs peuvent désormais effectuer en ligne leurs déclarations de devises et d'objets de valeur avant leur départ ou leur arrivée en Algérie, et télécharger directement les documents justificatifs. La plateforme permet également d'accéder aux différents services numériques proposés par les Douanes algériennes, notamment à un simulateur de calcul des droits et taxes applicables aux véhicules. Les voyageurs peuvent aussi consulter les taux de change officiels du dinar algérien face à plusieurs devises, dont l'euro, le dollar, le dirham des Émirats arabes unis, la livre sterling et le yuan chinois. Les démarches doivent être effectuées avant le départ ou l'arrivée en Algérie. La plateforme est accessible à l'adresse suivante : https://alces.douane.gov.dz/main . Avec l'ouverture d'ALCES aux particuliers, les douanes algériennes poursuivent la numérisation de leurs services afin de simplifier les démarches des voyageurs et de fluidifier les formalités aux frontières. L’article Voyage en Algérie : voici comment déclarer ses devises et objets de valeur est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Electricity: No tariff increase for now, says Power Minister
items.description: By Emeka Anaeto, Business Editor , & Sebastine Obasi Respite may have come the way of electricity consumers as Joseph Tegbe, the Minister of Power, yesterday announced that the Federal Government (FG) is not contemplating increase in electricity tariff for now. Making the clarification at a media interaction in Lagos yesterday, Tegbe stated: “Our priority is not tariff increase in the immediate term. Our objective is clear, to make electricity more available, make the grid more reliable, make the market financially sustainable and restore investor confidence. “We want to ensure that electricity becomes a catalyst for national productivity rather than a constraint to economic growth. “Indeed, the Federal Government will continue to examine additional mechanisms for protecting vulnerable consumers whilst simultaneously improving the financial sustainability of the market.” Tegbe, who took over leadership of the power sector as the minister 50 days ago, also gave insight on the grid audit he is embarking upon. He said: “Our first priority is the comprehensive technical audit of the transmission segment of our electricity network. “One cannot effectively rebuild what one has not properly diagnosed. The audit will identify ageing assets, overloaded substations, weak transmission corridors, protection failures, system bottlenecks and operational vulnerabilities. “This exercise will provide the factual basis for prioritising investments, reducing system failures, improving planning and ensuring that every naira invested delivers measurable value.” The Minister explained that the exercise will provide the factual basis for prioritising investments, reducing system failures, improving planning and ensuring that every naira invested delivers measurable value. According to him, “A stable grid is the foundation of reliable electricity. Consequently, we shall immediately commence strategic investments in three critical transmission corridors: Lagos Corridor; Enugu–Port Harcourt; and Abuja– Kaduna–Kano. Within the next 2-3 years, Nigerians should experience a stronger grid, reduced technical losses, improved market discipline, greater investor confidence, expanded electricity access and significantly higher operational capacity.” The post Electricity: No tariff increase for now, says Power Minister appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Sport, jeunesse et journalisme : Karim Baldé, le journaliste franco-africain se confie (Boubacar’s Substack)
items.description: Le journaliste franco-africain se livre sur les évènements sportifs et l’avenir du football. Boubacar Caba Bah Parcours et expériences de Karim Baldé . Karim Baldé est un journaliste français spécialisé dans le suivi des joueurs africains en Europe. Formé à Sciences Po (Paris) et à l’Université de Glendon de Toronto (Canada), Karim a couvert la Coupe du Monde 2022 pour la chaine de télévision TV5 Monde, obtenant des exclusivités sur les équipes africaines. Grâce à son double héritage guinéen et comorien, Karim Baldé a cofondé en 2016 l’émission radiophonique ToutFoot avec Hadafo, le groupe média du guinéen Lamine Guirassy. Dans ce balado – podcast Karim analyse les performances africaines, soulignant leur bon bilan en phase de groupes malgré leurs défaites en phase à élimination directe lors de la coupe du Monde. Karim a également couvert la finale de la Ligue des Champions d’Europe 2026 et la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations (CAN) au Maroc en 2026 ainsi que la CAN de Côte d’Ivoire 2021. Défis et solutions pour le football guinéen. Karim pointe les lacunes du football guinéen : instabilité de l’encadrement, manque de solutions tactiques, stades non homologués, et logistique défaillante, obligeant l’équipe nationale à jouer à l’étranger. Malgré ces défis, il note une amélioration à l’international de la couverture médiatique du football africain, notamment depuis la victoire de la Côte d’Ivoire à la CAN 2021. Il suggère aux autorités d’améliorer la gouvernance sportive en Guinée par une hiérarchie claire, la promotion d’autres disciplines, et l’acceptation de la critique constructive. Engagement et conseils Via son agence Bal des Productions , Karim produit des contenus sur le sport africain et forme de jeunes français. Aux jeunes aspirants journalistes en Guinée, il insiste sur la vérification des informations en allant sur les lieux des événements. Il conseille également aux jeunes Guinéens de se former localement avant de partir en Europe et admire les parcours d’anciennes gloires du football comme ceux du suédois Zlatan Ibrahimovic ou du guinéen Pascal Feindouno. Enfin, il prône l’optimisme et la diplomatie dans les critiques, une approche inspirée par son père. Ce balado / podcast de Boubacar Caba Bah dure environ 41 minutes. La transcription – cliquez sur la première icone ”Podcast” sur la photo – est également disponible. Il est aussi possible de visionner sur YouTube . Bonne écoute! items.title: Comment l’essor du tourisme récepteur reflète une Chine plus ouverte et plus connectée
items.description: Jin Shan Récemment, un événement de promotion du tourisme récepteur organisé sur les rives de la rivière Li à Guilin, célèbre destination touristique de la région autonome Zhuang du Guangxi (sud de la Chine), est devenu une excellente fenêtre pour observer la nouvelle tendance du tourisme récepteur en Chine : on y a vu Jackie Chan, ambassadeur du tourisme récepteur de Ctrip, rejoindre près de 2 000 acteurs mondiaux de l'industrie touristique pour partir en voyage dans les montagnes et les rivières. Le spectacle de drones a relié des motifs de films classiques à des sites de renom comme la rivière Li, les Montagnes Jaunes, la Tour de la Cloche de Xi'an et d'autres endroits de montagnes et de rivières. Lors de l'événement, un dirigeant de l'industrie touristique suisse s'est exclamé après avoir découvert l'artisanat de brocart du peuple Zhuang : « Le voyage est la meilleure clé pour éliminer les barrières culturelles et pour se comprendre mutuellement». Aujourd’hui, les expériences immersives sont devenues un élément standard du « menu » des voyages en Chine : à Zhangjiajie, dans la province du Hunan (centre de la Chine), des familles venues de l’étranger suivent des spécialistes des voyages sur mesure sur des sentiers pédestres ; dans les rues de Chongqing, les blogueurs étrangers aiment se plonger dans des feux d'artifice de saveurs sur les stands en bord de rue ; dans les vieilles rues de Tunxi, à Huangshan, dans la province de l’Anhui, les touristes russes découvrent l'architecture unique du Huizhou et découvrent la production d'encre de Huizhou… Aujourd’hui, les destinations du tourisme récepteur en Chine sont toujours plus diversifiées et les scénarios de voyage deviennent toujours plus riches. Les données montrent qu'au cours des quatre premiers mois de cette année, les exportations chinoises de services de voyage se sont élevées à 147,15 milliards de yuans, soit une augmentation de 30,4 % d’une année sur l’autre ; au premier trimestre, 8,315 millions d'étrangers sont entrés dans le pays sans visa, soit une augmentation de 29,3 % d’une année sur l’autre. Qu'il s'agisse de se promener pour voir des fleurs et des sites touristiques, ou d'assister à d’étonnantes surprises de la vie quotidienne ; qu'il s'agisse de « venir ici pour une visite » ou de vivre une expérience immersive de la vraie vie à la chinoise et de toucher la texture même de la culture chinoise, les nouveaux changements dans le tourisme récepteur reflètent la libération continue du potentiel de développement du commerce des services et sont également un exemple frappant de l'ouverture de haut niveau de la Chine sur le monde extérieur. La popularité du concept du « voyage en Chine » illustre l'attitude pragmatique de l'ouverture de la Chine. Le cercle des amis sans visa continue de s'élargir et les mesures de remboursement de taxes au départ sont encore optimisées… Diverses politiques d'ouverture sont mises en œuvre en détail pour améliorer continuellement la commodité d'entrée. Les services de l’industrie du tourisme culturel sont également de plus en plus internationalisés. À l'heure actuelle, plus de 150 000 commerçants touristiques nationaux ont accédé à la plateforme de version étrangère en 24 langues de Ctrip, réalisant ainsi une modernisation complète des capacités de réception entrante. En prenant Guilin comme exemple, les sites touristiques ont entièrement lancé des distributeurs de billets multilingues et des guides d'intelligence artificielle. Les hôtels ont amélioré l'affichage des installations multilingues en ligne, et des consultants spécialisés multilingues dédiés peuvent également créer des itinéraires d'expérience paysagère différenciés pour les touristes. Des systèmes d'affichage en ligne multilingues, une couverture complète du matériel de paiement en devises et des services de réception d'entrée standardisés ont consolidé les bases de l'industrie du tourisme récepteur. La popularité du concept du « voyage en Chine » montre aussi l'héritage culturel d'une Chine ouverte. Chacun peut ressentir le pouls de la modernisation grâce à des aéroports efficaces et ordonnés, un vaste réseau ferroviaire à grande vitesse et une infrastructure numérique avancée ; on peut visiter le musée des caractères chinois pour acquérir une compréhension détaillée de la méthode de création d'inscriptions d'oracle sur os et du développement des caractères chinois ; ou encore, en visitant l'ancienne ville de Zhaohua, on peut ressentir la continuation du contexte historique le long de l'ancienne route Shu et découvrir de manière immersive le charme des cultures des Trois Royaumes… La Chine, à la fois simple et riche, mais dynamique et tendance, attire de plus en plus de visiteurs du monde entier. Kevin Rotich, rédacteur en chef du site internet kényan Capital FM, a souligné que « la civilisation ancienne et l'innovation moderne se mélangent parfaitement ici… Je suis sincèrement émerveillé à chaque fois que j'en fais l'expérience ». La popularité du concept du « voyage en Chine » reflète encore les opportunités mondiales offertes par l'ouverture de la Chine. Le « Plan d'action pour la normalisation du commerce des services (2026-2030) » a été publié il n'y a pas si longtemps et se concentre clairement sur l'accélération de l'élaboration de normes dans les domaines des services touristiques et de la consommation entrante, et sur la promotion de l'intégration des normes de service avec les normes internationales avancées. En se concentrant sur l’élimination des goulots d’étranglement dans des domaines tels que les règles, les réglementations, la gestion et les normes, et en faisant progresser régulièrement l’ouverture institutionnelle donnera une impulsion importante à la construction d’une économie mondiale ouverte. Depuis le dévoilement de la zone franche pilote de Chine (Mongolie intérieure), jusqu'à la mise en œuvre complète des mesures de droits de douane nuls pour 53 pays africains entretenant des relations diplomatiques avec la Chine, en passant par le nombre de trains de marchandises Chine-Europe passant par le corridor, qui a dépassé 3 000 et ceux passant par le corridor central de la Chine qui a dépassé 2 000 depuis le début de cette année, un modèle d'ouverture tous azimuts, à plusieurs niveaux et sur une vaste zone a été accéléré. Le concept et les actions d'ouverture visant à promouvoir la coopération et le gagnant-gagnant sont profondément enracinés et portent désormais leurs fruits. Un blogueur américain a souligné après son voyage à Guilin que l'expérience du tourisme culturel est un dialogue sans barrières. Ce n’est qu’en permettant au monde d’entrer en personne en Chine que chacun pourra voir ce qu’est la vraie Chine. La culture et le tourisme peuvent être utilisés comme des moyens pour promouvoir les liens entre les peuples. La porte de la Chine vers l'ouverture s'ouvre de plus en plus largement, et l'ampleur et la profondeur des échanges et de l'apprentissage mutuel entre les civilisations continueront de s'élargir.

items.title: Religious scholar affiliated with JUI-F shot dead in Lower South Waziristan
items.description: LOWER SOUTH WAZIRISTAN: A religious scholar affiliated with the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F), Maulana Muhammad Ismail, was shot dead by unidentified armed men in the Azam Warsak area of Birmal tehsil in Lower South Waziristan, it emerged on Saturday. District Police Officer (DPO) Muhammad Tahir said that the incident occurred after Friday prayers when unidentified assailants on a motorcycle opened fire on Ismail, killing him on the spot. The official said the assailants managed to escape from the scene. The DPO said that an initial report of the incident had been registered and an investigation into the killing had been launched. He added that police were examining the incident from all angles. According to police officials and local tribal elders, the deceased was a resident of Kazha Panga and was serving as a teacher at a religious seminary in the area. In May, renowned cleric and former JUI-F MPA Maulana Muhammad Idrees was killed in Charsadda after unidentified assailants opened fire on him. In January, JUI-F leader Maulana Sultan Muhammad Wazir succumbed to his injuries after being critically wounded in a bomb blast near a madressah in South Waziristan’s Wana bazaar area.

items.title: New Army Divisions: Veterans split over timeline, funding fears
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA Retired military chiefs have cautioned President Bola Tinubu to fully resource the Nigerian Army’s existing eight divisions before pressing ahead with the newly approved expansion to twelve, warning that personnel and equipment gaps in the current formations, an unrealistic implementation timeline, and inadequate funding could undermine the initiative. Read Also: Gowon’s book of barefaced lies Former Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Lucky Irabor; former Air Force spokesperson, Group Captain Sadiq Shehu (retd); and former Joint Task Force (JTF) commander, retired Major General Anthony Atolagbe, raised the concerns in separate television interviews monitored in Abuja. They however commended the president’s decision to create four new divisions in Makurdi, Ilorin, Jalingo and Benin City, moving the Army’s force structure from eight to twelve. Irabor described the move as “a right step in the right direction” but insisted the existing formations must first be brought up to standard. “Increasing from 8 Divisions to 12 Divisions has a lot of implications. First, the existing 8 Divisions must be properly brought up to scale in terms of personnel, equipment, logistics, and so on and so forth,” he said. Shehu argued that the health of the current eight divisions had not been established before the decision to expand was taken. “What I had expected to be done, and I hope has been done, is to look at the existing eight divisions. How well resourced are they? Again, it is open knowledge that the military and even the ordinary citizens will be saying that the military is overstretched,” he said. He cited standard military benchmarks, known as Table of Organisation and Equipment TOE, which specify personnel and equipment levels for battalions, brigades and divisions. According to him, a battalion should typically have between 6,000 and 9,000 officers and men and requires roughly 750 rifles, dozens of vehicles and radios, along with communications and engineering equipment. “Unless you have this combination of organisation… and also equipment that is balanced, unless you have an appreciable number, your battalion, or your brigade, or your division is not going to function properly,” he said, adding that military scientists recommend units operate at 90 to 100 percent of TOE strength. Shehu also questioned the timeline set for the rollout, under which the 5th, 9th and 10th divisions are to be established by September 2026, with the 83rd division following by December. “With due respect, very good plan, but the timeline, again, is not realistic. It is very easy by presidential fiat to say, I have established a division, but to be honest, to have a ready division, in fact, even a ready brigade or a battalion within three months or five months is barely impossible.” He questioned how the announced recruitment of 28,000 additional personnel was expected to populate four new divisions, noting that a single division typically requires 15,000 to 20,000 officers and men, and warned that reassigning troops from existing units could dilute already under-strength formations. “If you have units that are already below TOE and you want to carry some of them and put them in new divisions, what you are doing? Again, you are diluting,” he said. Citing what he described as National Assembly disclosures attributed to Senator Ali Ndume, Shehu said the Army received less than five percent of its budget for equipment this year. “A unit without equipment is… you need the people. You need specialists, engineers, signals officers. All these are necessary to make a battalion a battalion,” he said, adding that pay alone would not resolve motivation gaps. “Certainly, the soldiers have been underpaid. We’ve heard that from a ridiculous N40,000, it has moved to N100,000. What will N100,000 achieve?” Shehu warned against treating the expansion as a political exercise disconnected from operational need. “Let’s not make it as if it is a politically kind of decision, that every area needs to have its division. That will not help the military. That will not help the country.” Atolagbe, however, offered a more optimistic reading of the same timeline, describing the overall expansion as one of the most far-reaching reorganisations of the military in recent memory. “I think what we are witnessing is what I will call a rejig at its best,” he said, adding later, “this is audacious,” when asked if it ranked among the most radical reforms of the Army to date. He explained that the new divisions were designed to close dangerous gaps in territorial coverage, particularly across the central belt of the country. “If you take the map of Nigeria based on what we used to have, you will notice that between the division that is in Sokoto and the one that is in Ilorin, there is a very big gap in terms of distance and space,” he said, warning that a fast-moving hostile force On the feasibility of the phased timeline, Atolagbe pushed back against suggestions that it was overly ambitious, noting that some proposed division headquarters, such as in Ilorin, already sit on existing barracks and battalions. “There’s what we call a task organisation now that will take place in such a way that if your battalion now is being taken over by another division, it means that they need to reallocate another battalion to you,” he said. On personnel, he noted that training timelines vary by rank, with recruits requiring about six months of training and officers up to four years at the Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA). “These are progressive steps that will be taken,” he said. items.title: Ghana’s creative industry must stop celebrating visibility and start building wealth
items.description: Ghana has never lacked creative talent. From highlife legends and Afrobeats pioneers to filmmakers, fashion designers and digital creators, the country has consistently produced ideas, stories and cultural expressions that influence the world. The challenge has never been creativity. The challenge has been building the systems, structures and business mindset needed to turn creativity into sustainable wealth. Ghana’s creative industry is currently experiencing a significant moment. Music is reaching global audiences, films are gaining recognition, fashion is shaping international conversations, and digital creators are using online platforms to build communities. The world is paying attention, with millions of views, growing audiences and viral moments becoming common. However, attention alone does not create wealth. Visibility does not guarantee ownership, and popularity does not automatically translate into financial security . A creator can become famous while remaining financially vulnerable. A song can dominate streaming platforms while someone else controls the rights. A skit can attract millions of viewers while the creator has limited control over how revenue is generated. The central question Ghana must confront is whether it is building a creative economy that creates owners, investors and successful businesses, or simply producing culture that others profit from . Applause is temporary. Ownership creates lasting value. The Problem With Chasing Virality The digital economy has transformed creativity. With a smartphone and an idea, anyone can reach audiences around the world. A song from a small studio can become a global hit, and a creator can build influence without traditional gatekeepers. However, this has also created the illusion that attention automatically equals success. It does not. A viral moment can fade quickly. Followers can increase while income remains stagnant. Popularity can grow while ownership remains uncertain. The more important question is not how many people saw a piece of content, but who benefited from that attention. Creative works are assets. A song is more than entertainment; it is intellectual property. A film is more than a story; it is a valuable catalogue. A fashion design is more than a product; it is the foundation of a potential brand. The challenge for Ghana is no longer proving that its creatives are talented. The challenge is ensuring that creators capture the economic value their talent produces. Creatives Must Think Like Owners For many years, creatives have been encouraged to focus on mastering their craft while paying less attention to business. Creating music, films, fashion and content is essential, but modern success requires more than artistic ability. The creative of the future must also be a strategist, entrepreneur and owner. An artiste should not only release songs; they should build a brand and manage a valuable catalogue of intellectual property. A film should not only win awards; it should generate long-term value. A fashion label should not only gain attention; it should develop into a scalable business. Global creative leaders understand this approach. They build ecosystems around their work through licensing, partnerships, investments, merchandise and ownership structures. Ghanaian creatives must begin asking deeper questions. Who owns the work? Who controls the revenue? Can this creation continue generating income years from now? The goal should not simply be to find the next opportunity. It should be to create lasting assets. The Industry Must Build the Invisible Infrastructure Ghana often celebrates the final creative product while overlooking the systems that make success possible. Audiences celebrate hit songs without discussing songwriters, publishers and rights management. They celebrate films without always recognising producers, writers and business teams. They admire fashion without examining the structures behind successful brands. Every strong creative economy depends on infrastructure. This includes publishers protecting rights, lawyers negotiating agreements, managers developing careers, investors providing capital, analysts understanding audiences and distributors connecting creators to global markets. Talent begins the journey, but infrastructure determines the outcome. Without these systems, Ghana risks producing exceptional creatives who remain financially dependent because they lack the tools to control and monetise their work. Building Ghana’s Creative Economy Machine Ghana does not need more talent. It needs stronger structures to transform talent into wealth. This requires better publishing systems that help creators understand and protect ownership. It requires stronger licensing frameworks so music, films, designs and stories continue generating revenue wherever they are used. It requires fair royalty systems that ensure creators are compensated when their work creates value. The industry must also embrace data-driven decision-making by understanding audiences, markets and consumer behaviour. Creative businesses need investment, not just project funding. Creatives need professional support systems so they are not forced to handle every role alone, from accounting and legal matters to marketing and business development. A successful creative economy is not created when everyone competes for attention. It is created when there is a strong system supporting those who receive attention. From Exporting Creativity to Building Wealth The world values African creativity, but admiration is not the same as ownership. If Ghana provides the music, stories, designs and ideas while others control distribution, platforms and profits, then the country is not fully building a creative economy. It is exporting creative labour. The same way countries have historically struggled when they exported raw resources without controlling the value chain, Ghana must avoid allowing its creativity to become another resource from which others gain the greatest benefit. The next resource being extracted is imagination. Those who create value must own a meaningful share of that value. The Future Belongs to Creative Owners Ghana does not need more evidence of its creative ability. The proof is already visible across the world. What is needed now is a shift in mindset. The next generation of creatives must understand contracts as well as creativity, intellectual property as well as trends, and business ownership as well as personal success. The true measure of Ghana’s creative success should not only be the number of people watching, listening to or following its creators. It should be the amount of wealth generated from that global attention. The creative revolution has already started. The next step is deciding whether Ghana will continue producing stars for the world to celebrate or build owners who shape the future.

items.title: How Delta Central APC meeting turned bloody
items.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi The National Anthem had just ended inside the PTI Conference Centre Hall, Effurun, last Sunday. Outside, at the bar and barbecue joint behind, bottles were already flying. By the time the echoes died, Senior Special Assistant to Governor Sheriff Oborevwori on Protocol, Simon Mudi, better known as Temple, lay dripping in blood, his head smashed repeatedly with bottles. Uvwie Local Government (LG) Chairman, Tony Ofoni and Commissioner for Works, Rueben Izeze, were also caught in the melee. Scores of APC faithful left with injuries. The meeting was convened to heal the party but at the end, the feud between two of the governor’s aides exploded into public view while the party tried to deny it. Our meeting, not our fight — APC Inside the hall, Delta Central APC leaders including Minister of Aviation, Festus Keyamo, Senator Ede Dafinone, Chief Ighoyota Amori, Stella Okotete, and LG chairmen had gathered for a stakeholders’ meeting to resolve differences instigated by divisive primaries and present a united front for 2027. The meeting ended peacefully. But outside the hall, it did not. Before guests would step out, a clash erupted at the sit-out bar behind the hall — where many party faithful who were denied entry had waited for their leaders. Temple, who moments before had manned the conference hall door to screen accredited invitees to the meeting, was the worst victim. Witnesses say bottles were repeatedly smashed on his head. From Okwagbe To Efurun: Feud in the making Sources say the violence was not spontaneous but the latest chapter in a running battle between Mudi and Izeze, both from Ughievwen sub-clan of Ughelli South LGA. The animosity, according to an APC chieftain, “became intense during consultations for the APC primary for Ughelli South House of Assembly. Mudi led leaders pushing for a consensus ticket for incumbent, Festus Utuama, claiming it was a directive of the Governor.” Izeze, leading those backing Emuobor Gbagi, fired back that the governor never gave such a directive and accused Mudi of “using the name of Oborevwori to tell a lie.” Ofoni, Uvwie LG Chairman, said the feud first boiled over “at Okwagbe during the funeral of the governor’s aide, Sunny Kotor” where the two allegedly clashed “in front of the Governor.” At PTI that fateful Sunday, Ofoni said he tried to settle the feud saying, “Temple and Izeze almost had a confrontation because of seats but I settled it before Izeze went outside of the meeting hall to make calls.” Minutes later, during the closing prayer, he (Ofoni) was told that they were fighting outside. “I ran outside, behold, two boys were lying down and another was running with blood dripping,” Ofoni said. Nursing his wounds at his Ekakpamre country home, Temple narrated, “I don’t know how a commissioner can set up another commissioner. On that day, he came with over 50 boys. I was on my way to eat with my watchmen. My associate called me that he saw a signal that they had brought a lot of boys to attack me. Immediately I dropped the call and saw about 12 boys who came to attack me. “Before I could say anything, they started breaking bottles everywhere, stabbing me everywhere. Everyone was running. I couldn’t even defend myself. It was when they saw the crowd coming that they stopped. It was a terrible experience. I just thank God for saving my life. As I am talking to you, my head was stitched in 11 different places.” Denial by the party 48 hours after, Delta APC’s response focused on optics. State Publicity Secretary, Valentine Onojeghuo, called media reports “reckless, false and sensational distortion.” He insisted that the meeting “was peaceful and concluded without any disruption” and that a viral video of chaos came “from another location within the expansive PTI complex. It is misleading and irresponsible to associate those unrelated scenes with the APC stakeholders’ meeting,” he said. Social media advocate, Zik Gbemre, in his reaction said, “Police were there watching like spectators as one thug before another smashed beer bottles on helpless Temple’s head and other victims. The real meeting may have ended without disruption, but it’s being clever by half to attempt to insinuate that the deadly fight involved a bunch of strangers unknown to the party. “Izeze and Temple can only deceive themselves. Nobody needs their validation to know the PTI mayhem was another ugly manifestation of their lingering feud. Even the governor knows. They fought in front of him in Okwagbe earlier. It is appalling that in the desperation to separate the party from the mayhem, the party muted names of key actors and victims. Delta APC showed the party’s name is far more valued than lives of members who were almost killed.” The Government steps in, police mute The State Government has however condemned the attack. Commissioner for Works and Public Information, Charles Aniagwu, said the “cruel attacks on Simon Mudi were unacceptable” and directed security agencies “to identify, arrest and prosecute those responsible.” But questions lingered about security. Ofoni confirmed that a legion of police from Ebrumede, Ekpan Divisions, Effurun Area Command and JTF were stationed in front of the meeting hall. According to him, “to them, they came to guard an APC meeting. Anyone killed outside was not their responsibility.” Days after, the Delta Police Command is yet to speak. Elders attempt to douse fire Wednesday, Ughievwen leaders met at Chief Patrick Fovie’s residence in Ughevwughe. They called for “immediate cessation of all forms of hostility” and set up a peace committee headed by Chief Fovie to “interface with the Governor to temper justice with mercy.” Chief Adelabu Bodjor, former Delta Central Chairman of the APC said both parties had agreed to resolve issues “amicably.” A unity meeting that exposed disunity The PTI Center meeting had all the right faces. It was broadcast live. The speeches were about cohesion. But behind the hall, bottles, blood and bruised egos told another story — of a party struggling to manage the ambitions of its own. As Mudi recuperates and investigations begin, one reality is clear: in Delta APC, the fight for 2027 may have already started and it is being fought among the governor’s own. The post How Delta Central APC meeting turned bloody appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ceuta | Miroir d’un monde déséquilibré
items.description: Les images de Ceuta **, l’enclave espagnole en terre africaine, reviennent régulièrement hanter les écrans. Des milliers de femmes, d’hommes et de jeunes franchissent une frontière, parfois au péril de leur vie, tandis que d’autres sont rapidement reconduits vers leur pays. L’actualité de ces derniers jours, avec des dizaines de milliers de passages suivis d’un retour massif vers le Maroc, rappelle une évidence : les migrations ne disparaissent jamais sous l’effet des seuls barbelés. Elles ne font que changer de visage. Khemaïs Gharbi * Le débat public se focalise souvent sur les chiffres, les contrôles aux frontières ou les conséquences politiques de ces mouvements. Pourtant, la véritable question est ailleurs : pourquoi tant de personnes sont-elles prêtes à quitter leur foyer, leur famille, leur culture et parfois leur dignité pour tenter leur chance de l’autre côté d’une frontière ? Le démographe et sociologue François Héran rappelle avec raison que l’immigration doit être abordée avec rigueur, en s’appuyant sur des faits plutôt que sur les émotions ou les slogans. Les données méritent d’être examinées avec précision, sans exagération ni minimisation. C’est à cette condition que le débat démocratique peut échapper aux caricatures et aux surenchères populistes, qui font le lit de l'extrême droite raciste et xénophobe en Europe. La richesse mondiale répartie de manière inégale Mais derrière les statistiques se cache une réalité plus profonde. Depuis des décennies, la richesse mondiale est répartie de manière profondément inégale. Une partie importante de l’humanité demeure exclue des bénéfices de la mondialisation, alors même que les moyens de communication lui montrent quotidiennement le niveau de vie auquel elle n’a pas accès. L’Afrique paie un tribut particulièrement lourd à cette injustice. Continent riche en ressources naturelles, en jeunesse et en potentiel humain, elle continue pourtant à voir une partie de ses enfants chercher ailleurs ce qu’ils ne trouvent pas chez eux : un emploi, un avenir, une sécurité ou simplement l’espoir d’une vie meilleure. Aucun mur, aucune clôture, aucune politique de refoulement ne pourra durablement contenir une espérance plus forte que la peur. L’histoire de l’humanité montre que les migrations accompagnent les grands déséquilibres économiques et politiques. Elles en sont souvent la conséquence plus que la cause. La véritable réponse ne réside donc pas uniquement dans le renforcement des frontières. Elle suppose un effort international beaucoup plus ambitieux en faveur du développement, de l’éducation, de la stabilité politique, de la création d’emplois et d’un partage plus équitable des richesses. Permettre à chacun de vivre dignement dans son pays reste la politique migratoire la plus humaine, la plus efficace et la moins coûteuse à long terme. Pour un ordre international plus juste Tant que les écarts de richesse continueront de se creuser entre les régions du monde, les mouvements migratoires resteront une réalité durable. On pourra en modifier les itinéraires, en ralentir les flux ou en déplacer les points de passage, mais on n’en supprimera jamais les causes profondes. Les événements de Ceuta ne constituent donc pas une exception. Ils sont le symptôme d’un monde dont les déséquilibres n’ont jamais été véritablement corrigés. Tant que cette injustice perdurera, la migration demeurera moins un problème à résoudre qu’un appel à construire un ordre international plus juste. * Ecrivain et traducteur. ** Entre le 30 et le 31 juillet 2026, près de 50 000 à 60 000 migrants, en grande majorité des jeunes hommes et des adolescents, ont traversé illégalement la frontière depuis le Maroc, en forçant le passage par la terre et par la mer dans des conditions chaotiques. Cet afflux massif, marqué par des dizaines de morts en mer, a entraîné l’envoi de l’armée par Madrid et un renforcement des contrôles frontaliers en Europe. L’article Ceuta | Miroir d’un monde déséquilibré est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .
